The majority read ﴿wa-l-habbu dhu al-'asfi wa-r-rayhan﴾ with all three in the nominative, coordinated with the nominative preceding them. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi 'Abla read all three in the accusative, meaning: and He created the grain. They permitted that "al-rayhan" be in the nominative or the accusative with an omitted modifier, meaning: and the possessor of the rayhan, omitting the modifier and putting the modifier-of-it in its place. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and al-Asma'i from Abu 'Amr read "wa-r-rayhani" in the genitive, and the meaning is: the grain that has husks, which is the fodder of beasts, and the rayhan, which is the food of people. The inclusion of the fragrant in the genitive reading is far-fetched. "Rayhan" is from the roots with a waw. Abu 'Ali permitted that it be a noun used in place of a verbal noun, and that it be a verbal noun of the pattern fa'lan, like al-labban. The waw was changed to a ya', just as they changed the ya' to a waw in ashawa. Or it is an irregular verbal noun from a defective root, as the irregular forms bununah and buynunah occur. Its original form is rayawhan; the waw was changed to a ya' and assimilated into the ya', becoming rayyhan, then the middle radical of the word was deleted, as they said: mayt and hayn.

When God, exalted is He, enumerated His blessings, He addressed the two weighty ones with His saying: ﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 32]. That is: His blessings are many and cannot be counted, so which of them will you deny? That is, one whose blessings are these cannot deny them. This address was to the two weighty ones, because both are included among the creatures according to the most correct opinions. This is also in keeping with His saying: ﴿He created man﴾ and ﴿and He created the jinn﴾, and with His saying: ﴿We will attend to you, O two weighty ones﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 31]. He who made it an address to males and females of the children of Adam has gone too far. Even further is the saying of one who said: it is an address in the manner of His saying: ﴿Cast into Hell﴾ [Qaf: 24], and "O my guard, strike his neck," meaning that it is an address to one person in the form of two. Then "fa-bi-ayyi" is tanwin in the whole surah, as if the genitive complement were omitted from it, and "ala'i rabbikuma" was substituted for it as a substitute of a definite from an indefinite. "Ala'" was previously stated in al-A'raf to mean blessings, its singular forms being ilyun, alan, ilan and alyun.

﴿He created man﴾: when He mentioned the greater world of the heaven and earth, and what He brought into existence in them of blessings, He mentioned the origin of the one for whom these blessings were created. "Al-insan" is Adam, and this is the view of the majority. It was said: it is the genus, and that was permissible because their father was created from clay. If by "al-insan" Adam is meant, then he passed through different stages, due to the transformation of his origin: he was first dust, then clay, then black mud molded, then dry clay. So it was appropriate that his creation be attributed to each of these. "Al-jann" is the father of the jinn, and he is Iblis, according to al-Hasan. Mujahid said: he is the father of the jinn, and not Iblis. It was said: "al-jann" is a generic noun. "Al-marij" is what is mixed of yellow, red and green, or the flame, or the pure, or the redness at the edge of the fire, or what is mixed with blackness, or what moves without smoke: these are opinions. ("Min") in the first is for the starting point of the end, and the second ("min nar") is partitive. It was said it is for explanation. The repetition in these refrains is for emphasis, alerting and stirring, and it appears in several places in the Qur'an. Some people, including Ibn Qutaybah, went to the view that this repetition is only for the variety of blessings, so He repeated the reminder (al-tawqif) for each one of them.

Al-Jumhur read "rabbu" and "rabbu" in the nominative, meaning: He is Lord. Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi 'Abla read it in the genitive as a substitute for "rabbikuma." He used the dual for the genitive complement because they are the two rising-places of summer and winter and their two setting-places, said Mujahid. It was said: the two rising-places of the sun and the moon and their two setting-places. From Ibn Abbas: the sun has a rising-place in summer that is high, and a rising-place in winter that is low, moving between them, rising and descending. He concluded. So the two rising-places and the two setting-places belong to the sun. It was said: the two rising-places are the dawn's rising and the sun's rising, and the two setting-places are the setting of twilight and the setting of the sun. Sahl al-Tustari has words about the two rising-places and the two setting-places resembling the words of the Batiniyyah, who distort the meaning of God's speech, which we pass over without mention. Likewise what we have come across of the words of the extremists who are attributed to the Sufis, since we do not consider it lawful to relate anything from it. The author of the book al-Tahrir wa-l-Tahbir has gone to excess, according to what these extremists said, in every verse, and he calls that "realities" (haqa'iq). The lords of hearts and what they claimed to understand from the Qur'an, they went to excess in it, and no Arab ever understood it, nor did God intend it by those words. We seek refuge in God from that.

﴿He let loose the two seas, meeting﴾: the discussion of this has preceded in al-Furqan. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-Tha'labi mentioned in ﴿He let loose the two seas﴾ riddles and esoteric sayings to which none should pay attention. He concluded. The apparent meaning is that they meet, that is, they are adjacent, so there is no separation between the two waters in the sight of the eye. It was said: they meet once every year. It was said: they are prepared for meeting, so their right is that they meet, were it not for a barrier between them.

﴿A barrier﴾: that is, a separation from the power of God, exalted is He. ﴿They do not transgress﴾: they do not exceed their limit, and neither of them oversteps the other by mixing. It was said: the barrier is the bodies of the earth, said by Qatadah. It was said: "la yabghiyan" means over people and habitation, and according to this and the previous, it is from "baghy" (oppression). It was said: it is from baghā, meaning to seek; the meaning is: they do not seek a state other than that in which they were created and subjugated. It was said: the water of rivers does not mix with salt water, but remains in itself within it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: observation does not require this. He concluded, meaning that one observes sweet water mixing with salt so that all of it becomes salt. It may be said: by mixing, the particles of the sweet water change until they are not apparent, and when a person tastes from the salt spread within it those fine particles, he perceives only the saltiness, and reason testifies to this, because the interpenetration of bodies is impossible, but separation and meeting are possible. The judge Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballluti, may God have mercy on him, recited:

Mixed waters, where the sweet does not prevail over the salt in goodness, nor does the salt become sweet.

The Jumhur read ﴿yakhruju﴾ with the active voice. Nafi', Abu 'Amr and the people of Madina read it in the passive voice. Al-Ju'fi, from Abu 'Amr, read it with a ya' vowelled with a damma and a kasra on the ra', meaning "Allah brings forth." From him, and from Abu 'Amr and Ibn Miqsam, it is also reported with a nun. In these two readings, "al-lu'lu'" (pearl) and "al-marjan" (coral) are in the accusative case. The apparent sense of ﴿minhuma﴾ ("from both of them") is that these come out of the salt and the sweet waters together. This was said by a group of people, reported by al-Akhfash. Others rejected this view, saying that sensory observation contradicts it, since pearls only come out of salt water. They also criticised the line of the poet:

*"He brought you whatever you wished, a perfume-caravan, / with the waters of the Euphrates surging over its face."*

The Jumhur said that pearls come out of the brackish water only in the places where rivers and sweet waters flow into the sea. So it was fitting to attribute the emergence to both. This is well known among pearl divers. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah said that these things are found in the sea through the descent of rain, because the oyster and other shellfish open their mouths to the rain. Therefore He said "from both of them." Abu 'Ubayda said that they come out of the salt water only, but He said "from both" by way of metonymy (tajawwuz). Al-Rummani said that the sweet water in them is like the fertilising agent for the salt water. It is like what is said: "The child comes out of the male and the female."

Ibn 'Atiyya, following al-Zajjaj, said: since they are one kind, the emergence of these things is indeed from both of them, even though in detail it is specifically from one of them. He said, as in ﴿seven heavens, layered﴾ [Nuh: 15] and ﴿and placed the moon in them as a light﴾ [Nuh: 16], while it is only in one of them, which is the lowest, the world. Al-Zamakhshari said something close to Ibn 'Atiyya's view. He said: If you ask, "Why did He say 'from both of them' when they only come out of the salt water?" I answer: when the two waters meet and become like one thing, it is permissible to say "they come out of both of them," just as one says "they come out of the sea," though they do not come out of the whole sea but from a part of it. And you say, "I left the town," when you have left only one quarter of its quarters, indeed only one house of its houses. It was also said: they only come out from the meeting place of the salt and the sweet waters. End of quotation.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: this is of the type of omission of a noun (hadhf al-mudaf), and the sense is "it comes out of one of the two," as in His words ﴿a great man from the two towns﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31], meaning "from one of the two towns." It was also said: they are two seas. From one comes out pearls and from the other comes coral.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the words of Allah the Exalted deserve more consideration than the words of some people. Who has informed you that pearls do not come out of sweet water? Suppose the divers only brought them out from salt water. But why do you say that the oyster does not come out, by Allah's command, from sweet water into salt water? How can one be certain of this, when apparent earthly matters are hidden from merchants who have crossed deserts and traveled the lands? How then could something at the bottom of the sea be hidden from them?

As for "al-lu'lu'," Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Qatada said it refers to large pearls, and "al-marjan" to small ones. Also from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali and Murra al-Hamdani, the reverse is reported. Abu 'Abd Allah and Abu Malik said: "al-marjan" is the red stone. Al-Zajjaj said it is a very white stone. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la related that it is a kind of pearl, like branches. "Al-marjan" is a non-Arabic word that has been Arabised. Ibn Durayd said: I have not heard it in any inflected form. Al-A'sha said:

*"Out of every marjana in the sea, its current preserved it, / and the shell protected it from its clay."*

It was said that he meant a large pearl. Talha read "al-lu'li" with a kasra on the third letter, and this is a dialect. 'Abd al-Wali: the final hamza is changed into a quiescent ya' after a kasra preceding it. This is a dialect, as stated by Abu al-Fadl al-Razi.

﴿And His are the ships﴾: He specified the ships as belonging to Him, although the heavens, the earth and what is in them all belong to Him. Because they were the ones who created them, He attributed them to Himself, since the complete benefit of them comes from Him, the Exalted. So He is in reality their owner. Al-jawari means the ships. 'Abd Allah, al-Hasan and 'Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr read it with a damma on the ra', as they say "shakin" becomes "shakkun." The Jumhur read ﴿al-munshatu﴾ with a fatha on the shin, as a passive participle, meaning either that Allah created them, or the people did, or that they are ships with raised sails. Mujahid said: whatever has a sail is among the "munshat," and whatever has no sail raised is not among the "munshat." Al-shira' means the sail. Al-A'mash, Hamza, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Talha and Abu Bakr, with a variant from him, read it with a kasra on the shin, meaning "the ones raising sails," or "the ones that generate the waves by their running," or "the ones that generate the journey, going forward and backward." Ibn Abi 'Abla and al-Hasan read it with a shadda on the shin, "al-munsha'ah," and this makes the adjective definite and indicates the plural noun described, as in His words ﴿purified spouses﴾ [al-Baqara: 25]. The hamza was changed into an alif, on the pattern of the line:

*"Indeed the beasts of prey are at rest in their lairs."*

He means "latahda'" (they rest). The ta' is the feminine marker of the adjective, written as ta' according to its pronunciation in connected speech.

﴿Like mountains (al-a'lam)﴾: that is, like mountains and hills. This indicates the size of the ships, since He likened them to mountains, although "munshat" applies both to large and to small ships. He used "man" in His words ﴿everyone on it﴾ to give precedence to those who have reason (taghlib). The pronoun in ﴿'alayha﴾ ("on it") refers, rarely, to the earth in His words ﴿and the earth, He laid it out for the creatures﴾. So the pronoun returned to it, although it came after its word.

"Fana'" (passing away) is an expression for the annihilation of all existing things, animals and others. "Wajh" (face) is used to express the essence of a thing. The bodily organ is negated of Allah the Exalted, as in ﴿everything perishes except His face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]. The beggars of Mecca say: "Where is the face of a noble Arab who will be generous to me?"

The Jumhur read ﴿dhu﴾ with a waw, as an adjective of "wajh." Ubayy and 'Abd Allah read ﴿dhi﴾ with a ya', as an adjective of "Rabb" (Lord). The apparent sense is that the address in ﴿the face of your Lord﴾ is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and in it there is a great honour for him (ﷺ). It was also said that the address is to every listener.

The meaning of ﴿dhu al-jalal﴾ (Possessor of majesty) is the One whom those who affirm His oneness (al-muwahhidun) glorify, by not likening Him to His creation or to their actions. Or it means He is the One at whom one marvels for His majesty. Or it means the One who has majesty and honour for His sincere servants.

﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him﴾: that is, their needs. This includes what concerns those in the heavens regarding the matter of religion and what they are made to serve, and what concerns those on earth regarding their religion and their worldly affairs. Abu Salih said: those in the heavens ask for mercy, and those on earth ask for forgiveness and provision. Ibn Jurayj said: the angels ask for provision for the people of the earth and forgiveness, and the people of the earth ask for both together. The apparent sense is that His words ﴿yas'aluhu﴾ are a resumptive statement of information (istinaf ikhbar). It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the "face," and its governing element is "yabqa" (remains), meaning that He is constantly in this state. This is what was said, and there is distance in it. Whoever does not ask, his state calls for asking. So it is valid to attribute the asking to all, on the basis of the shared quality, which is their need of Him, the Exalted.

﴿Every day﴾: that is, every hour and every moment. He mentioned "day" because the hours and moments are included within it.

﴿He is in a matter﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: in a matter that He carries out concerning creation, provision, giving life and causing death. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: He answers one who calls, relieves one who is distressed, accepts repentance from one people, and forgives another people. Suwayd ibn Ghafla said: He frees necks, gives to the needy, and imposes punishment. Ibn 'Uyayna said: With Allah, time consists of two days. One is the day that is the duration of the world, and in it His matter is command and prohibition, death and life. The second is the Day of Resurrection, and in it His matter is requital and reckoning. From Muqatil: it was revealed about the Jews, who said: "Allah does not decree anything on Saturday." Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl, when 'Abd Allah ibn Tahir asked him about His words ﴿every day He is in a matter﴾, while it is established that the pen has dried with what will be until the Day of Resurrection, said: "They are matters that He manifests, not matters that He initiates." Ibn Bahr said: He is in the day of the world in trial, and in the Day of Resurrection in requital.

﴿Every day﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf). Its governing element is the element governing ﴿in a matter﴾, which is the implied stable predicate (al-mustaqirr al-mahdhuf), like "on Friday, Zayd is standing."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 55, verses 7–30 (part 1 of 2):

When God, exalted is He, mentioned the benefit of the sun and the moon, which He had bestowed, and this was among the heavenly signs (al-ayat al-'ulwiyyah), He mentioned in contrast to them the earthly effects (al-athar al-sufl































































iyyah): the star (al-najm) and the tree (al-shajar), since these two are provision for mankind. He also informed that the sun and the moon run as God willed for them, by His subjugating them and by their existence as His wisdom required, exalted is He. When He mentioned that by which the spirits live, which is the teaching of the Qur'an, He mentioned that by which the bodies live, which is the plants that have a stalk (saq). The star, which has no stalk, was placed first because it is the root of sustenance, while that which has a stalk is generally the one whose fruit is eaten for enjoyment. The apparent meaning is that the star is what we have explained, and this is indicated by its being paired with the tree. Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Hasan said: "al-najm" is a generic noun referring to the stars of the sky. As for their prostration (sujud), Mujahid and al-Hasan said: for the star it is by its setting and the like, and for the tree it is by its shadow and its turning. Mujahid also said: "prostration" is a figurative usage, an expression for submission and humbling oneself. The first clauses (al-jumal al-ula) contain a pronoun that connects them to the subject (al-mubtada'), whereas in these two clauses he relied on the semantic connection (al-wasl al-ma'nawi) rather than the verbal connection (al-wasl al-lafzi), since it is known that the reckoning (al-husban) is His reckoning and that the prostration is to Him and not to other than Him. It is as if it were said: "by His reckoning, and they prostrate to Him." When these clauses were presented in the context of enumerating blessings, the discourse reverted to coordination (al-'atf) in joining what is suitable to join with it. The suitability between these two clauses is evident, since the sun and the moon are heavenly, and the star and the tree are earthly.

﴿And the sky, He raised it﴾: that is, He created it raised up, in that He made it the source of His decrees and the dwelling of His angels who descend with revelation to His prophets, and by this He draws attention to the greatness of His station and His dominion. The majority read "wa-s-sama'a" in the accusative by way of al-ishtighal (the construction in which a verb is suppressed and a pronoun-object is pre-posed, i.e., a verb governing the noun is implied), observing harmony with the clause that follows it, which is ﴿yasjudan﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 6]. Abu al-Sammal read "wa-s-sama'u" in the nominative, observing harmony with the nominal (ibtida'iyyah) clause. The majority read ﴿wa-wada'a al-mizan﴾ as a past verb governing "al-mizan" in the accusative, meaning He established and fixed it. Ibrahim read "wa-wad'i al-mizan" in the genitive with a sukun on the dad. The apparent meaning is that it is everything by which things are weighed and their quantities known, even if the instruments differ. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah said this: He made Him, exalted is He, a judge with equity in giving and taking. Mujahid, al-Tabari and most scholars said: "al-mizan" is justice (al-'adl), and the instruments are among what falls under justice. He began first with knowledge, mentioning that which contains the noblest kinds of knowledge, which is the Qur'an; then He mentioned that by which things are made equitable, which is the balance, as in His saying: ﴿And We sent down with them the Book and the balance﴾ [al-Hadid: 25], so that they might teach the Book and do what the Book commands them. (That you not transgress in the balance): that is, so that you do not transgress, where "tatghaw" is in the accusative governed by "an" (the particle meaning "that"). Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is "an" the explanatory (al-mufassirah, the explanatory "an" which introduces an explanation of a preceding clause containing a sense of saying). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "an" may be explanatory, so that "tatghaw" would be jussive by the prohibition. He concluded. What these two said, that "an" is explanatory, is not permissible, because one of its two conditions is missing, namely that the clause preceding it must be a clause containing the meaning of speech.

﴿And He set up the balance﴾ is a clause that does not contain the meaning of speech. Transgression in the balance is that it be done deliberately, but as for what one cannot measure accurately with the balance, that is pardoned.

Since equity is very much desired, God, exalted is He, commanded, saying: ﴿And establish the weight﴾. The majority read ﴿wa-la tukhsiru﴾ (and do not make deficient), from akhsara, meaning to corrupt and diminish, as in His saying: ﴿And when they measure for others or weigh for them, they cause loss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 3]; that is, they diminish. Bilal ibn Abi Burdah and Zayd ibn 'Ali read "takhsaru" with a fathah on the ta', said: khasira yakhsaru and akhsara yukhsiru have one meaning, like jabara and ajbara. Ibn Jinni and the author of al-Lawami' related from Bilal the reading "takhsaru" with a fathah on the ta' and the sin, as the present of khasira with a kasrah on the sin. Al-Zamakhshari explained it as meaning: "in the balance," so the preposition was omitted and the noun put in the accusative, but this explanation is unnecessary. Do you not see that khasira is used transitively, as in His saying: ﴿They have lost themselves﴾ [al-An'am: 12], and ﴿He has lost the world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Hajj: 11]? It was also read "takhsuru," with a fathah on the ta' and a dammah on the sin. Since excess was forbidden, namely transgression, He forbade loss, which is deficiency, and He repeated the word "al-mizan" to emphasize the injunction concerning it and to strengthen the command to use it and urge it.

When He mentioned the sky, He mentioned its counterpart, saying: ﴿And the earth, He laid it out for the creatures﴾: that is, He spread it out (khafadha), extended upon the water, so that it may be benefited from. The majority read "wa-l-ard" in the accusative; Abu al-Sammal read it in the nominative, "wa-l-anamu." Ibn Abbas said: "al-anam" means the children of Adam only. He also said, as did Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and al-Sha'bi: it is all animal life. Al-Hasan said: it is the two weighty ones (al-thaqalan), jinn and humankind.

﴿In it is fruit﴾: kinds of things by which one takes enjoyment. He began with "fakihah" (fruit), since it is of the mode of beginning with the lowest and ascending to the highest. He made its word indefinite because the benefit of it is less than the benefit of what is mentioned after it. Then he followed with the palm, mentioning the root and not mentioning its fruit, which is the dates, because of the great benefit of it: from fiber, palm fronds, branches, trunks, the heart of the palm (al-jummar), and dates. Then he came third with the grain, which is the support of human life in most regions, namely wheat, barley, and everything that has an ear of grain and branching leaves on its stalk. He described it with His saying ﴿possessing husks﴾ (dhu al-'asf), as a reminder of His favor upon them by what sustains them of grain, and what sustains their beasts from its leaves, which is the straw. He began with the fruit and ended with the fragrant, and between them were the palm and the grain, so that there would be what is enjoyed, what is eaten for sustenance, and what gives the pleasure of a good scent. He mentioned the palm by its name and the fruit without its tree, because of the great benefit of the palm from several aspects, while the fruit-tree is contemptible in comparison to its fruit; so He specified what the benefit of the palm tree and of fruit is greatest in, rather than the trees of fruit.

The majority read ﴿wa-l-habbu dhu al-'asfi wa-r-rayhan﴾ with all three in the nominative, coordinated with the nominative preceding them. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi 'Abla read all three in the accusative, meaning: and He created the grain. They permitted that "al-rayhan" be in the nominative or the accusative with an omitted modifier, meaning: and the possessor of the rayhan, omitting the modifier and putting the modifier-of-it in its place. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and al-Asma'i from Abu 'Amr read "wa-r-rayhani" in the genitive, and the meaning is: the grain that has husks, which is the fodder of beasts, and the rayhan, which is the food of people. The inclusion of the fragrant in the genitive reading is far-fetched. "Rayhan" is from the roots with a waw. Abu 'Ali permitted that it be a noun used in place of a verbal noun, and that it be a verbal noun of the pattern fa'lan, like al-labban. The waw was changed to a ya', just as they changed the ya' to a waw in ashawa. Or it is an irregular verbal noun from a defective root, as the irregular forms bununah and buynunah occur. Its original form is rayawhan; the waw was changed to a ya' and assimilated into the ya', becoming rayyhan, then the middle radical of the word was deleted, as they said: mayt and hayn.

When God, exalted is He, enumerated His blessings, He addressed the two weighty ones with His saying: ﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 32]. That is: His blessings are many and cannot be counted, so which of them will you deny? That is, one whose blessings are these cannot deny them. This address was to the two weighty ones, because both are included among the creatures according to the most correct opinions. This is also in keeping with His saying: ﴿He created man﴾ and ﴿and He created the jinn﴾, and with His saying: ﴿We will attend to you, O two weighty ones﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 31]. He who made it an address to males and females of the children of Adam has gone too far. Even further is the saying of one who said: it is an address in the manner of His saying: ﴿Cast into Hell﴾ [Qaf: 24], and "O my guard, strike his neck," meaning that it is an address to one person in the form of two. Then "fa-bi-ayyi" is tanwin in the whole surah, as if the genitive complement were omitted from it, and "ala'i rabbikuma" was substituted for it as a substitute of a definite from an indefinite. "Ala'" was previously stated in al-A'raf to mean blessings, its singular forms being ilyun, alan, ilan and alyun.

﴿He created man﴾: when He mentioned the greater world of the heaven and earth, and what He brought into existence in them of blessings, He mentioned the origin of the one for whom these blessings were created. "Al-insan" is Adam, and this is the view of the majority. It was said: it is the genus, and that was permissible because their father was created from clay. If by "al-insan" Adam is meant, then he passed through different stages, due to the transformation of his origin: he was first dust, then clay, then black mud molded, then dry clay. So it was appropriate that his creation be attributed to each of these. "Al-jann" is the father of the jinn, and he is Iblis, according to al-Hasan. Mujahid said: he is the father of the jinn, and not Iblis. It was said: "al-jann" is a generic noun. "Al-marij" is what is mixed of yellow, red and green, or the flame, or the pure, or the redness at the edge of the fire, or what is mixed with blackness, or what moves without smoke: these are opinions. ("Min") in the first is for the starting point of the end, and the second ("min nar") is partitive. It was said it is for explanation. The repetition in these refrains is for emphasis, alerting and stirring, and it appears in several places in the Qur'an. Some people, including Ibn Qutaybah, went to the view that this repetition is only for the variety of blessings, so He repeated the reminder (al-tawqif) for each one of them.

Al-Jumhur read "rabbu" and "rabbu" in the nominative, meaning: He is Lord. Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi 'Abla read it in the genitive as a substitute for "rabbikuma." He used the dual for the genitive complement because they are the two rising-places of summer and winter and their two setting-places, said Mujahid. It was said: the two rising-places of the sun and the moon and their two setting-places. From Ibn Abbas: the sun has a rising-place in summer that is high, and a rising-place in winter that is low, moving between them, rising and descending. He concluded. So the two rising-places and the two setting-places belong to the sun. It was said: the two rising-places are the dawn's rising and the sun's rising, and the two setting-places are the setting of twilight and the setting of the sun. Sahl al-Tustari has words about the two rising-places and the two setting-places resembling the words of the Batiniyyah, who distort the meaning of God's speech, which we pass over without mention. Likewise what we have come across of the words of the extremists who are attributed to the Sufis, since we do not consider it lawful to relate anything from it. The author of the book al-Tahrir wa-l-Tahbir has gone to excess, according to what these extremists said, in every verse, and he calls that "realities" (haqa'iq). The lords of hearts and what they claimed to understand from the Qur'an, they went to excess in it, and no Arab ever understood it, nor did God intend it by those words. We seek refuge in God from that.

﴿He let loose the two seas, meeting﴾: the discussion of this has preceded in al-Furqan. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-Tha'labi mentioned in ﴿He let loose the two seas﴾ riddles and esoteric sayings to which none should pay attention. He concluded. The apparent meaning is that they meet, that is, they are adjacent, so there is no separation between the two waters in the sight of the eye. It was said: they meet once every year. It was said: they are prepared for meeting, so their right is that they meet, were it not for a barrier between them.

﴿A barrier﴾: that is, a separation from the power of God, exalted is He. ﴿They do not transgress﴾: they do not exceed their limit, and neither of them oversteps the other by mixing. It was said: the barrier is the bodies of the earth, said by Qatadah. It was said: "la yabghiyan" means over people and habitation, and according to this and the previous, it is from "baghy" (oppression). It was said: it is from baghā, meaning to seek; the meaning is: they do not seek a state other than that in which they were created and subjugated. It was said: the water of rivers does not mix with salt water, but remains in itself within it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: observation does not require this. He concluded, meaning that one observes sweet water mixing with salt so that all of it becomes salt. It may be said: by mixing, the particles of the sweet water change until they are not apparent, and when a person tastes from the salt spread within it those fine particles, he perceives only the saltiness, and reason testifies to this, because the interpenetration of bodies is impossible, but separation and meeting are possible. The judge Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballluti, may God have mercy on him, recited:

Mixed waters, where the sweet does not prevail over the salt in goodness, nor does the salt become sweet.

The Jumhur read ﴿yakhruju﴾ with the active voice. Nafi', Abu 'Amr and the people of Madina read it in the passive voice. Al-Ju'fi, from Abu 'Amr, read it with a ya' vowelled with a damma and a kasra on the ra', meaning "Allah brings forth." From him, and from Abu 'Amr and Ibn Miqsam, it is also reported with a nun. In these two readings, "al-lu'lu'" (pearl) and "al-marjan" (coral) are in the accusative case. The apparent sense of ﴿minhuma﴾ ("from both of them") is that these come out of the salt and the sweet waters together. This was said by a group of people, reported by al-Akhfash. Others rejected this view, saying that sensory observation contradicts it, since pearls only come out of salt water. They also criticised the line of the poet:

*"He brought you whatever you wished, a perfume-caravan, / with the waters of the Euphrates surging over its face."*

The Jumhur said that pearls come out of the brackish water only in the places where rivers and sweet waters flow into the sea. So it was fitting to attribute the emergence to both. This is well known among pearl divers. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah said that these things are found in the sea through the descent of rain, because the oyster and other shellfish open their mouths to the rain. Therefore He said "from both of them." Abu 'Ubayda said that they come out of the salt water only, but He said "from both" by way of metonymy (tajawwuz). Al-Rummani said that the sweet water in them is like the fertilising agent for the salt water. It is like what is said: "The child comes out of the male and the female."

Ibn 'Atiyya, following al-Zajjaj, said: since they are one kind, the emergence of these things is indeed from both of them, even though in detail it is specifically from one of them. He said, as in ﴿seven heavens, layered﴾ [Nuh: 15] and ﴿and placed the moon in them as a light﴾ [Nuh: 16], while it is only in one of them, which is the lowest, the world. Al-Zamakhshari said something close to Ibn 'Atiyya's view. He said: If you ask, "Why did He say 'from both of them' when they only come out of the salt water?" I answer: when the two waters meet and become like one thing, it is permissible to say "they come out of both of them," just as one says "they come out of the sea," though they do not come out of the whole sea but from a part of it. And you say, "I left the town," when you have left only one quarter of its quarters, indeed only one house of its houses. It was also said: they only come out from the meeting place of the salt and the sweet waters. End of quotation.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: this is of the type of omission of a noun (hadhf al-mudaf), and the sense is "it comes out of one of the two," as in His words ﴿a great man from the two towns﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31], meaning "from one of the two towns." It was also said: they are two seas. From one comes out pearls and from the other comes coral.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the words of Allah the Exalted deserve more consideration than the words of some people. Who has informed you that pearls do not come out of sweet water? Suppose the divers only brought them out from salt water. But why do you say that the oyster does not come out, by Allah's command, from sweet water into salt water? How can one be certain of this, when apparent earthly matters are hidden from merchants who have crossed deserts and traveled the lands? How then could something at the bottom of the sea be hidden from them?

As for "al-lu'lu'," Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Qatada said it refers to large pearls, and "al-marjan" to small ones. Also from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali and Murra al-Hamdani, the reverse is reported. Abu 'Abd Allah and Abu Malik said: "al-marjan" is the red stone. Al-Zajjaj said it is a very white stone. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la related that it is a kind of pearl, like branches. "Al-marjan" is a non-Arabic word that has been Arabised. Ibn Durayd said: I have not heard it in any inflected form. Al-A'sha said:

*"Out of every marjana in the sea, its current preserved it, / and the shell protected it from its clay."*

It was said that he meant a large pearl. Talha read "al-lu'li" with a kasra on the third letter, and this is a dialect. 'Abd al-Wali: the final hamza is changed into a quiescent ya' after a kasra preceding it. This is a dialect, as stated by Abu al-Fadl al-Razi.

﴿And His are the ships﴾: He specified the ships as belonging to Him, although the heavens, the earth and what is in them all belong to Him. Because they were the ones who created them, He attributed them to Himself, since the complete benefit of them comes from Him, the Exalted. So He is in reality their owner. Al-jawari means the ships. 'Abd Allah, al-Hasan and 'Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr read it with a damma on the ra', as they say "shakin" becomes "shakkun." The Jumhur read ﴿al-munshatu﴾ with a fatha on the shin, as a passive participle, meaning either that Allah created them, or the people did, or that they are ships with raised sails. Mujahid said: whatever has a sail is among the "munshat," and whatever has no sail raised is not among the "munshat." Al-shira' means the sail. Al-A'mash, Hamza, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Talha and Abu Bakr, with a variant from him, read it with a kasra on the shin, meaning "the ones raising sails," or "the ones that generate the waves by their running," or "the ones that generate the journey, going forward and backward." Ibn Abi 'Abla and al-Hasan read it with a shadda on the shin, "al-munsha'ah," and this makes the adjective definite and indicates the plural noun described, as in His words ﴿purified spouses﴾ [al-Baqara: 25]. The hamza was changed into an alif, on the pattern of the line:

*"Indeed the beasts of prey are at rest in their lairs."*

He means "latahda'" (they rest). The ta' is the feminine marker of the adjective, written as ta' according to its pronunciation in connected speech.

﴿Like mountains (al-a'lam)﴾: that is, like mountains and hills. This indicates the size of the ships, since He likened them to mountains, although "munshat" applies both to large and to small ships. He used "man" in His words ﴿everyone on it﴾ to give precedence to those who have reason (taghlib). The pronoun in ﴿'alayha﴾ ("on it") refers, rarely, to the earth in His words ﴿and the earth, He laid it out for the creatures﴾. So the pronoun returned to it, although it came after its word.

"Fana'" (passing away) is an expression for the annihilation of all existing things, animals and others. "Wajh" (face) is used to express the essence of a thing. The bodily organ is negated of Allah the Exalted, as in ﴿everything perishes except His face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]. The beggars of Mecca say: "Where is the face of a noble Arab who will be generous to me?"

The Jumhur read ﴿dhu﴾ with a waw, as an adjective of "wajh." Ubayy and 'Abd Allah read ﴿dhi﴾ with a ya', as an adjective of "Rabb" (Lord). The apparent sense is that the address in ﴿the face of your Lord﴾ is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and in it there is a great honour for him (ﷺ). It was also said that the address is to every listener.

The meaning of ﴿dhu al-jalal﴾ (Possessor of majesty) is the One whom those who affirm His oneness (al-muwahhidun) glorify, by not likening Him to His creation or to their actions. Or it means He is the One at whom one marvels for His majesty. Or it means the One who has majesty and honour for His sincere servants.

﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him﴾: that is, their needs. This includes what concerns those in the heavens regarding the matter of religion and what they are made to serve, and what concerns those on earth regarding their religion and their worldly affairs. Abu Salih said: those in the heavens ask for mercy, and those on earth ask for forgiveness and provision. Ibn Jurayj said: the angels ask for provision for the people of the earth and forgiveness, and the people of the earth ask for both together. The apparent sense is that His words ﴿yas'aluhu﴾ are a resumptive statement of information (istinaf ikhbar). It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the "face," and its governing element is "yabqa" (remains), meaning that He is constantly in this state. This is what was said, and there is distance in it. Whoever does not ask, his state calls for asking. So it is valid to attribute the asking to all, on the basis of the shared quality, which is their need of Him, the Exalted.

﴿Every day﴾: that is, every hour and every moment. He mentioned "day" because the hours and moments are included within it.

﴿He is in a matter﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: in a matter that He carries out concerning creation, provision, giving life and causing death. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: He answers one who calls, relieves one who is distressed, accepts repentance from one people, and forgives another people. Suwayd ibn Ghafla said: He frees necks, gives to the needy, and imposes punishment. Ibn 'Uyayna said: With Allah, time consists of two days. One is the day that is the duration of the world, and in it His matter is command and prohibition, death and life. The second is the Day of Resurrection, and in it His matter is requital and reckoning. From Muqatil: it was revealed about the Jews, who said: "Allah does not decree anything on Saturday." Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl, when 'Abd Allah ibn Tahir asked him about His words ﴿every day He is in a matter﴾, while it is established that the pen has dried with what will be until the Day of Resurrection, said: "They are matters that He manifests, not matters that He initiates." Ibn Bahr said: He is in the day of the world in trial, and in the Day of Resurrection in requital.

﴿Every day﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf). Its governing element is the element governing ﴿in a matter﴾, which is the implied stable predicate (al-mustaqirr al-mahdhuf), like "on Friday, Zayd is standing."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 55, verses 7–30 (part 1 of 2):

When God, exalted is He, mentioned the benefit of the sun and the moon, which He had bestowed, and this was among the heavenly signs (al-ayat al-'ulwiyyah), He mentioned in contrast to them the earthly effects (al-athar al-sufl































































iyyah): the star (al-najm) and the tree (al-shajar), since these two are provision for mankind. He also informed that the sun and the moon run as God willed for them, by His subjugating them and by their existence as His wisdom required, exalted is He. When He mentioned that by which the spirits live, which is the teaching of the Qur'an, He mentioned that by which the bodies live, which is the plants that have a stalk (saq). The star, which has no stalk, was placed first because it is the root of sustenance, while that which has a stalk is generally the one whose fruit is eaten for enjoyment. The apparent meaning is that the star is what we have explained, and this is indicated by its being paired with the tree. Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Hasan said: "al-najm" is a generic noun referring to the stars of the sky. As for their prostration (sujud), Mujahid and al-Hasan said: for the star it is by its setting and the like, and for the tree it is by its shadow and its turning. Mujahid also said: "prostration" is a figurative usage, an expression for submission and humbling oneself. The first clauses (al-jumal al-ula) contain a pronoun that connects them to the subject (al-mubtada'), whereas in these two clauses he relied on the semantic connection (al-wasl al-ma'nawi) rather than the verbal connection (al-wasl al-lafzi), since it is known that the reckoning (al-husban) is His reckoning and that the prostration is to Him and not to other than Him. It is as if it were said: "by His reckoning, and they prostrate to Him." When these clauses were presented in the context of enumerating blessings, the discourse reverted to coordination (al-'atf) in joining what is suitable to join with it. The suitability between these two clauses is evident, since the sun and the moon are heavenly, and the star and the tree are earthly.

﴿And the sky, He raised it﴾: that is, He created it raised up, in that He made it the source of His decrees and the dwelling of His angels who descend with revelation to His prophets, and by this He draws attention to the greatness of His station and His dominion. The majority read "wa-s-sama'a" in the accusative by way of al-ishtighal (the construction in which a verb is suppressed and a pronoun-object is pre-posed, i.e., a verb governing the noun is implied), observing harmony with the clause that follows it, which is ﴿yasjudan﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 6]. Abu al-Sammal read "wa-s-sama'u" in the nominative, observing harmony with the nominal (ibtida'iyyah) clause. The majority read ﴿wa-wada'a al-mizan﴾ as a past verb governing "al-mizan" in the accusative, meaning He established and fixed it. Ibrahim read "wa-wad'i al-mizan" in the genitive with a sukun on the dad. The apparent meaning is that it is everything by which things are weighed and their quantities known, even if the instruments differ. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah said this: He made Him, exalted is He, a judge with equity in giving and taking. Mujahid, al-Tabari and most scholars said: "al-mizan" is justice (al-'adl), and the instruments are among what falls under justice. He began first with knowledge, mentioning that which contains the noblest kinds of knowledge, which is the Qur'an; then He mentioned that by which things are made equitable, which is the balance, as in His saying: ﴿And We sent down with them the Book and the balance﴾ [al-Hadid: 25], so that they might teach the Book and do what the Book commands them. (That you not transgress in the balance): that is, so that you do not transgress, where "tatghaw" is in the accusative governed by "an" (the particle meaning "that"). Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is "an" the explanatory (al-mufassirah, the explanatory "an" which introduces an explanation of a preceding clause containing a sense of saying). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "an" may be explanatory, so that "tatghaw" would be jussive by the prohibition. He concluded. What these two said, that "an" is explanatory, is not permissible, because one of its two conditions is missing, namely that the clause preceding it must be a clause containing the meaning of speech.

﴿And He set up the balance﴾ is a clause that does not contain the meaning of speech. Transgression in the balance is that it be done deliberately, but as for what one cannot measure accurately with the balance, that is pardoned.

Since equity is very much desired, God, exalted is He, commanded, saying: ﴿And establish the weight﴾. The majority read ﴿wa-la tukhsiru﴾ (and do not make deficient), from akhsara, meaning to corrupt and diminish, as in His saying: ﴿And when they measure for others or weigh for them, they cause loss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 3]; that is, they diminish. Bilal ibn Abi Burdah and Zayd ibn 'Ali read "takhsaru" with a fathah on the ta', said: khasira yakhsaru and akhsara yukhsiru have one meaning, like jabara and ajbara. Ibn Jinni and the author of al-Lawami' related from Bilal the reading "takhsaru" with a fathah on the ta' and the sin, as the present of khasira with a kasrah on the sin. Al-Zamakhshari explained it as meaning: "in the balance," so the preposition was omitted and the noun put in the accusative, but this explanation is unnecessary. Do you not see that khasira is used transitively, as in His saying: ﴿They have lost themselves﴾ [al-An'am: 12], and ﴿He has lost the world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Hajj: 11]? It was also read "takhsuru," with a fathah on the ta' and a dammah on the sin. Since excess was forbidden, namely transgression, He forbade loss, which is deficiency, and He repeated the word "al-mizan" to emphasize the injunction concerning it and to strengthen the command to use it and urge it.

When He mentioned the sky, He mentioned its counterpart, saying: ﴿And the earth, He laid it out for the creatures﴾: that is, He spread it out (khafadha), extended upon the water, so that it may be benefited from. The majority read "wa-l-ard" in the accusative; Abu al-Sammal read it in the nominative, "wa-l-anamu." Ibn Abbas said: "al-anam" means the children of Adam only. He also said, as did Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and al-Sha'bi: it is all animal life. Al-Hasan said: it is the two weighty ones (al-thaqalan), jinn and humankind.

﴿In it is fruit﴾: kinds of things by which one takes enjoyment. He began with "fakihah" (fruit), since it is of the mode of beginning with the lowest and ascending to the highest. He made its word indefinite because the benefit of it is less than the benefit of what is mentioned after it. Then he followed with the palm, mentioning the root and not mentioning its fruit, which is the dates, because of the great benefit of it: from fiber, palm fronds, branches, trunks, the heart of the palm (al-jummar), and dates. Then he came third with the grain, which is the support of human life in most regions, namely wheat, barley, and everything that has an ear of grain and branching leaves on its stalk. He described it with His saying ﴿possessing husks﴾ (dhu al-'asf), as a reminder of His favor upon them by what sustains them of grain, and what sustains their beasts from its leaves, which is the straw. He began with the fruit and ended with the fragrant, and between them were the palm and the grain, so that there would be what is enjoyed, what is eaten for sustenance, and what gives the pleasure of a good scent. He mentioned the palm by its name and the fruit without its tree, because of the great benefit of the palm from several aspects, while the fruit-tree is contemptible in comparison to its fruit; so He specified what the benefit of the palm tree and of fruit is greatest in, rather than the trees of fruit.

The majority read ﴿wa-l-habbu dhu al-'asfi wa-r-rayhan﴾ with all three in the nominative, coordinated with the nominative preceding them. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi 'Abla read all three in the accusative, meaning: and He created the grain. They permitted that "al-rayhan" be in the nominative or the accusative with an omitted modifier, meaning: and the possessor of the rayhan, omitting the modifier and putting the modifier-of-it in its place. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and al-Asma'i from Abu 'Amr read "wa-r-rayhani" in the genitive, and the meaning is: the grain that has husks, which is the fodder of beasts, and the rayhan, which is the food of people. The inclusion of the fragrant in the genitive reading is far-fetched. "Rayhan" is from the roots with a waw. Abu 'Ali permitted that it be a noun used in place of a verbal noun, and that it be a verbal noun of the pattern fa'lan, like al-labban. The waw was changed to a ya', just as they changed the ya' to a waw in ashawa. Or it is an irregular verbal noun from a defective root, as the irregular forms bununah and buynunah occur. Its original form is rayawhan; the waw was changed to a ya' and assimilated into the ya', becoming rayyhan, then the middle radical of the word was deleted, as they said: mayt and hayn.

When God, exalted is He, enumerated His blessings, He addressed the two weighty ones with His saying: ﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 32]. That is: His blessings are many and cannot be counted, so which of them will you deny? That is, one whose blessings are these cannot deny them. This address was to the two weighty ones, because both are included among the creatures according to the most correct opinions. This is also in keeping with His saying: ﴿He created man﴾ and ﴿and He created the jinn﴾, and with His saying: ﴿We will attend to you, O two weighty ones﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 31]. He who made it an address to males and females of the children of Adam has gone too far. Even further is the saying of one who said: it is an address in the manner of His saying: ﴿Cast into Hell﴾ [Qaf: 24], and "O my guard, strike his neck," meaning that it is an address to one person in the form of two. Then "fa-bi-ayyi" is tanwin in the whole surah, as if the genitive complement were omitted from it, and "ala'i rabbikuma" was substituted for it as a substitute of a definite from an indefinite. "Ala'" was previously stated in al-A'raf to mean blessings, its singular forms being ilyun, alan, ilan and alyun.

﴿He created man﴾: when He mentioned the greater world of the heaven and earth, and what He brought into existence in them of blessings, He mentioned the origin of the one for whom these blessings were created. "Al-insan" is Adam, and this is the view of the majority. It was said: it is the genus, and that was permissible because their father was created from clay. If by "al-insan" Adam is meant, then he passed through different stages, due to the transformation of his origin: he was first dust, then clay, then black mud molded, then dry clay. So it was appropriate that his creation be attributed to each of these. "Al-jann" is the father of the jinn, and he is Iblis, according to al-Hasan. Mujahid said: he is the father of the jinn, and not Iblis. It was said: "al-jann" is a generic noun. "Al-marij" is what is mixed of yellow, red and green, or the flame, or the pure, or the redness at the edge of the fire, or what is mixed with blackness, or what moves without smoke: these are opinions. ("Min") in the first is for the starting point of the end, and the second ("min nar") is partitive. It was said it is for explanation. The repetition in these refrains is for emphasis, alerting and stirring, and it appears in several places in the Qur'an. Some people, including Ibn Qutaybah, went to the view that this repetition is only for the variety of blessings, so He repeated the reminder (al-tawqif) for each one of them.

Al-Jumhur read "rabbu" and "rabbu" in the nominative, meaning: He is Lord. Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi 'Abla read it in the genitive as a substitute for "rabbikuma." He used the dual for the genitive complement because they are the two rising-places of summer and winter and their two setting-places, said Mujahid. It was said: the two rising-places of the sun and the moon and their two setting-places. From Ibn Abbas: the sun has a rising-place in summer that is high, and a rising-place in winter that is low, moving between them, rising and descending. He concluded. So the two rising-places and the two setting-places belong to the sun. It was said: the two rising-places are the dawn's rising and the sun's rising, and the two setting-places are the setting of twilight and the setting of the sun. Sahl al-Tustari has words about the two rising-places and the two setting-places resembling the words of the Batiniyyah, who distort the meaning of God's speech, which we pass over without mention. Likewise what we have come across of the words of the extremists who are attributed to the Sufis, since we do not consider it lawful to relate anything from it. The author of the book al-Tahrir wa-l-Tahbir has gone to excess, according to what these extremists said, in every verse, and he calls that "realities" (haqa'iq). The lords of hearts and what they claimed to understand from the Qur'an, they went to excess in it, and no Arab ever understood it, nor did God intend it by those words. We seek refuge in God from that.

﴿He let loose the two seas, meeting﴾: the discussion of this has preceded in al-Furqan. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-Tha'labi mentioned in ﴿He let loose the two seas﴾ riddles and esoteric sayings to which none should pay attention. He concluded. The apparent meaning is that they meet, that is, they are adjacent, so there is no separation between the two waters in the sight of the eye. It was said: they meet once every year. It was said: they are prepared for meeting, so their right is that they meet, were it not for a barrier between them.

﴿A barrier﴾: that is, a separation from the power of God, exalted is He. ﴿They do not transgress﴾: they do not exceed their limit, and neither of them oversteps the other by mixing. It was said: the barrier is the bodies of the earth, said by Qatadah. It was said: "la yabghiyan" means over people and habitation, and according to this and the previous, it is from "baghy" (oppression). It was said: it is from baghā, meaning to seek; the meaning is: they do not seek a state other than that in which they were created and subjugated. It was said: the water of rivers does not mix with salt water, but remains in itself within it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: observation does not require this. He concluded, meaning that one observes sweet water mixing with salt so that all of it becomes salt. It may be said: by mixing, the particles of the sweet water change until they are not apparent, and when a person tastes from the salt spread within it those fine particles, he perceives only the saltiness, and reason testifies to this, because the interpenetration of bodies is impossible, but separation and meeting are possible. The judge Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballluti, may God have mercy on him, recited:

Mixed waters, where the sweet does not prevail over the salt in goodness, nor does the salt become sweet.

The Jumhur read ﴿yakhruju﴾ with the active voice. Nafi', Abu 'Amr and the people of Madina read it in the passive voice. Al-Ju'fi, from Abu 'Amr, read it with a ya' vowelled with a damma and a kasra on the ra', meaning "Allah brings forth." From him, and from Abu 'Amr and Ibn Miqsam, it is also reported with a nun. In these two readings, "al-lu'lu'" (pearl) and "al-marjan" (coral) are in the accusative case. The apparent sense of ﴿minhuma﴾ ("from both of them") is that these come out of the salt and the sweet waters together. This was said by a group of people, reported by al-Akhfash. Others rejected this view, saying that sensory observation contradicts it, since pearls only come out of salt water. They also criticised the line of the poet:

*"He brought you whatever you wished, a perfume-caravan, / with the waters of the Euphrates surging over its face."*

The Jumhur said that pearls come out of the brackish water only in the places where rivers and sweet waters flow into the sea. So it was fitting to attribute the emergence to both. This is well known among pearl divers. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah said that these things are found in the sea through the descent of rain, because the oyster and other shellfish open their mouths to the rain. Therefore He said "from both of them." Abu 'Ubayda said that they come out of the salt water only, but He said "from both" by way of metonymy (tajawwuz). Al-Rummani said that the sweet water in them is like the fertilising agent for the salt water. It is like what is said: "The child comes out of the male and the female."

Ibn 'Atiyya, following al-Zajjaj, said: since they are one kind, the emergence of these things is indeed from both of them, even though in detail it is specifically from one of them. He said, as in ﴿seven heavens, layered﴾ [Nuh: 15] and ﴿and placed the moon in them as a light﴾ [Nuh: 16], while it is only in one of them, which is the lowest, the world. Al-Zamakhshari said something close to Ibn 'Atiyya's view. He said: If you ask, "Why did He say 'from both of them' when they only come out of the salt water?" I answer: when the two waters meet and become like one thing, it is permissible to say "they come out of both of them," just as one says "they come out of the sea," though they do not come out of the whole sea but from a part of it. And you say, "I left the town," when you have left only one quarter of its quarters, indeed only one house of its houses. It was also said: they only come out from the meeting place of the salt and the sweet waters. End of quotation.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: this is of the type of omission of a noun (hadhf al-mudaf), and the sense is "it comes out of one of the two," as in His words ﴿a great man from the two towns﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31], meaning "from one of the two towns." It was also said: they are two seas. From one comes out pearls and from the other comes coral.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the words of Allah the Exalted deserve more consideration than the words of some people. Who has informed you that pearls do not come out of sweet water? Suppose the divers only brought them out from salt water. But why do you say that the oyster does not come out, by Allah's command, from sweet water into salt water? How can one be certain of this, when apparent earthly matters are hidden from merchants who have crossed deserts and traveled the lands? How then could something at the bottom of the sea be hidden from them?

As for "al-lu'lu'," Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Qatada said it refers to large pearls, and "al-marjan" to small ones. Also from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali and Murra al-Hamdani, the reverse is reported. Abu 'Abd Allah and Abu Malik said: "al-marjan" is the red stone. Al-Zajjaj said it is a very white stone. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la related that it is a kind of pearl, like branches. "Al-marjan" is a non-Arabic word that has been Arabised. Ibn Durayd said: I have not heard it in any inflected form. Al-A'sha said:

*"Out of every marjana in the sea, its current preserved it, / and the shell protected it from its clay."*

It was said that he meant a large pearl. Talha read "al-lu'li" with a kasra on the third letter, and this is a dialect. 'Abd al-Wali: the final hamza is changed into a quiescent ya' after a kasra preceding it. This is a dialect, as stated by Abu al-Fadl al-Razi.

﴿And His are the ships﴾: He specified the ships as belonging to Him, although the heavens, the earth and what is in them all belong to Him. Because they were the ones who created them, He attributed them to Himself, since the complete benefit of them comes from Him, the Exalted. So He is in reality their owner. Al-jawari means the ships. 'Abd Allah, al-Hasan and 'Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr read it with a damma on the ra', as they say "shakin" becomes "shakkun." The Jumhur read ﴿al-munshatu﴾ with a fatha on the shin, as a passive participle, meaning either that Allah created them, or the people did, or that they are ships with raised sails. Mujahid said: whatever has a sail is among the "munshat," and whatever has no sail raised is not among the "munshat." Al-shira' means the sail. Al-A'mash, Hamza, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Talha and Abu Bakr, with a variant from him, read it with a kasra on the shin, meaning "the ones raising sails," or "the ones that generate the waves by their running," or "the ones that generate the journey, going forward and backward." Ibn Abi 'Abla and al-Hasan read it with a shadda on the shin, "al-munsha'ah," and this makes the adjective definite and indicates the plural noun described, as in His words ﴿purified spouses﴾ [al-Baqara: 25]. The hamza was changed into an alif, on the pattern of the line:

*"Indeed the beasts of prey are at rest in their lairs."*

He means "latahda'" (they rest). The ta' is the feminine marker of the adjective, written as ta' according to its pronunciation in connected speech.

﴿Like mountains (al-a'lam)﴾: that is, like mountains and hills. This indicates the size of the ships, since He likened them to mountains, although "munshat" applies both to large and to small ships. He used "man" in His words ﴿everyone on it﴾ to give precedence to those who have reason (taghlib). The pronoun in ﴿'alayha﴾ ("on it") refers, rarely, to the earth in His words ﴿and the earth, He laid it out for the creatures﴾. So the pronoun returned to it, although it came after its word.

"Fana'" (passing away) is an expression for the annihilation of all existing things, animals and others. "Wajh" (face) is used to express the essence of a thing. The bodily organ is negated of Allah the Exalted, as in ﴿everything perishes except His face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]. The beggars of Mecca say: "Where is the face of a noble Arab who will be generous to me?"

The Jumhur read ﴿dhu﴾ with a waw, as an adjective of "wajh." Ubayy and 'Abd Allah read ﴿dhi﴾ with a ya', as an adjective of "Rabb" (Lord). The apparent sense is that the address in ﴿the face of your Lord﴾ is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and in it there is a great honour for him (ﷺ). It was also said that the address is to every listener.

The meaning of ﴿dhu al-jalal﴾ (Possessor of majesty) is the One whom those who affirm His oneness (al-muwahhidun) glorify, by not likening Him to His creation or to their actions. Or it means He is the One at whom one marvels for His majesty. Or it means the One who has majesty and honour for His sincere servants.

﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him﴾: that is, their needs. This includes what concerns those in the heavens regarding the matter of religion and what they are made to serve, and what concerns those on earth regarding their religion and their worldly affairs. Abu Salih said: those in the heavens ask for mercy, and those on earth ask for forgiveness and provision. Ibn Jurayj said: the angels ask for provision for the people of the earth and forgiveness, and the people of the earth ask for both together. The apparent sense is that His words ﴿yas'aluhu﴾ are a resumptive statement of information (istinaf ikhbar). It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the "face," and its governing element is "yabqa" (remains), meaning that He is constantly in this state. This is what was said, and there is distance in it. Whoever does not ask, his state calls for asking. So it is valid to attribute the asking to all, on the basis of the shared quality, which is their need of Him, the Exalted.

﴿Every day﴾: that is, every hour and every moment. He mentioned "day" because the hours and moments are included within it.

﴿He is in a matter﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: in a matter that He carries out concerning creation, provision, giving life and causing death. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: He answers one who calls, relieves one who is distressed, accepts repentance from one people, and forgives another people. Suwayd ibn Ghafla said: He frees necks, gives to the needy, and imposes punishment. Ibn 'Uyayna said: With Allah, time consists of two days. One is the day that is the duration of the world, and in it His matter is command and prohibition, death and life. The second is the Day of Resurrection, and in it His matter is requital and reckoning. From Muqatil: it was revealed about the Jews, who said: "Allah does not decree anything on Saturday." Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl, when 'Abd Allah ibn Tahir asked him about His words ﴿every day He is in a matter﴾, while it is established that the pen has dried with what will be until the Day of Resurrection, said: "They are matters that He manifests, not matters that He initiates." Ibn Bahr said: He is in the day of the world in trial, and in the Day of Resurrection in requital.

﴿Every day﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf). Its governing element is the element governing ﴿in a matter﴾, which is the implied stable predicate (al-mustaqirr al-mahdhuf), like "on Friday, Zayd is standing."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 55, verses 7–30 (part 1 of 2):

When God, exalted is He, mentioned the benefit of the sun and the moon, which He had bestowed, and this was among the heavenly signs (al-ayat al-'ulwiyyah), He mentioned in contrast to them the earthly effects (al-athar al-sufl































































iyyah): the star (al-najm) and the tree (al-shajar), since these two are provision for mankind. He also informed that the sun and the moon run as God willed for them, by His subjugating them and by their existence as His wisdom required, exalted is He. When He mentioned that by which the spirits live, which is the teaching of the Qur'an, He mentioned that by which the bodies live, which is the plants that have a stalk (saq). The star, which has no stalk, was placed first because it is the root of sustenance, while that which has a stalk is generally the one whose fruit is eaten for enjoyment. The apparent meaning is that the star is what we have explained, and this is indicated by its being paired with the tree. Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Hasan said: "al-najm" is a generic noun referring to the stars of the sky. As for their prostration (sujud), Mujahid and al-Hasan said: for the star it is by its setting and the like, and for the tree it is by its shadow and its turning. Mujahid also said: "prostration" is a figurative usage, an expression for submission and humbling oneself. The first clauses (al-jumal al-ula) contain a pronoun that connects them to the subject (al-mubtada'), whereas in these two clauses he relied on the semantic connection (al-wasl al-ma'nawi) rather than the verbal connection (al-wasl al-lafzi), since it is known that the reckoning (al-husban) is His reckoning and that the prostration is to Him and not to other than Him. It is as if it were said: "by His reckoning, and they prostrate to Him." When these clauses were presented in the context of enumerating blessings, the discourse reverted to coordination (al-'atf) in joining what is suitable to join with it. The suitability between these two clauses is evident, since the sun and the moon are heavenly, and the star and the tree are earthly.

﴿And the sky, He raised it﴾: that is, He created it raised up, in that He made it the source of His decrees and the dwelling of His angels who descend with revelation to His prophets, and by this He draws attention to the greatness of His station and His dominion. The majority read "wa-s-sama'a" in the accusative by way of al-ishtighal (the construction in which a verb is suppressed and a pronoun-object is pre-posed, i.e., a verb governing the noun is implied), observing harmony with the clause that follows it, which is ﴿yasjudan﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 6]. Abu al-Sammal read "wa-s-sama'u" in the nominative, observing harmony with the nominal (ibtida'iyyah) clause. The majority read ﴿wa-wada'a al-mizan﴾ as a past verb governing "al-mizan" in the accusative, meaning He established and fixed it. Ibrahim read "wa-wad'i al-mizan" in the genitive with a sukun on the dad. The apparent meaning is that it is everything by which things are weighed and their quantities known, even if the instruments differ. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah said this: He made Him, exalted is He, a judge with equity in giving and taking. Mujahid, al-Tabari and most scholars said: "al-mizan" is justice (al-'adl), and the instruments are among what falls under justice. He began first with knowledge, mentioning that which contains the noblest kinds of knowledge, which is the Qur'an; then He mentioned that by which things are made equitable, which is the balance, as in His saying: ﴿And We sent down with them the Book and the balance﴾ [al-Hadid: 25], so that they might teach the Book and do what the Book commands them. (That you not transgress in the balance): that is, so that you do not transgress, where "tatghaw" is in the accusative governed by "an" (the particle meaning "that"). Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is "an" the explanatory (al-mufassirah, the explanatory "an" which introduces an explanation of a preceding clause containing a sense of saying). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "an" may be explanatory, so that "tatghaw" would be jussive by the prohibition. He concluded. What these two said, that "an" is explanatory, is not permissible, because one of its two conditions is missing, namely that the clause preceding it must be a clause containing the meaning of speech.

﴿And He set up the balance﴾ is a clause that does not contain the meaning of speech. Transgression in the balance is that it be done deliberately, but as for what one cannot measure accurately with the balance, that is pardoned.

Since equity is very much desired, God, exalted is He, commanded, saying: ﴿And establish the weight﴾. The majority read ﴿wa-la tukhsiru﴾ (and do not make deficient), from akhsara, meaning to corrupt and diminish, as in His saying: ﴿And when they measure for others or weigh for them, they cause loss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 3]; that is, they diminish. Bilal ibn Abi Burdah and Zayd ibn 'Ali read "takhsaru" with a fathah on the ta', said: khasira yakhsaru and akhsara yukhsiru have one meaning, like jabara and ajbara. Ibn Jinni and the author of al-Lawami' related from Bilal the reading "takhsaru" with a fathah on the ta' and the sin, as the present of khasira with a kasrah on the sin. Al-Zamakhshari explained it as meaning: "in the balance," so the preposition was omitted and the noun put in the accusative, but this explanation is unnecessary. Do you not see that khasira is used transitively, as in His saying: ﴿They have lost themselves﴾ [al-An'am: 12], and ﴿He has lost the world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Hajj: 11]? It was also read "takhsuru," with a fathah on the ta' and a dammah on the sin. Since excess was forbidden, namely transgression, He forbade loss, which is deficiency, and He repeated the word "al-mizan" to emphasize the injunction concerning it and to strengthen the command to use it and urge it.

When He mentioned the sky, He mentioned its counterpart, saying: ﴿And the earth, He laid it out for the creatures﴾: that is, He spread it out (khafadha), extended upon the water, so that it may be benefited from. The majority read "wa-l-ard" in the accusative; Abu al-Sammal read it in the nominative, "wa-l-anamu." Ibn Abbas said: "al-anam" means the children of Adam only. He also said, as did Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and al-Sha'bi: it is all animal life. Al-Hasan said: it is the two weighty ones (al-thaqalan), jinn and humankind.

﴿In it is fruit﴾: kinds of things by which one takes enjoyment. He began with "fakihah" (fruit), since it is of the mode of beginning with the lowest and ascending to the highest. He made its word indefinite because the benefit of it is less than the benefit of what is mentioned after it. Then he followed with the palm, mentioning the root and not mentioning its fruit, which is the dates, because of the great benefit of it: from fiber, palm fronds, branches, trunks, the heart of the palm (al-jummar), and dates. Then he came third with the grain, which is the support of human life in most regions, namely wheat, barley, and everything that has an ear of grain and branching leaves on its stalk. He described it with His saying ﴿possessing husks﴾ (dhu al-'asf), as a reminder of His favor upon them by what sustains them of grain, and what sustains their beasts from its leaves, which is the straw. He began with the fruit and ended with the fragrant, and between them were the palm and the grain, so that there would be what is enjoyed, what is eaten for sustenance, and what gives the pleasure of a good scent. He mentioned the palm by its name and the fruit without its tree, because of the great benefit of the palm from several aspects, while the fruit-tree is contemptible in comparison to its fruit; so He specified what the benefit of the palm tree and of fruit is greatest in, rather than the trees of fruit.

The majority read ﴿wa-l-habbu dhu al-'asfi wa-r-rayhan﴾ with all three in the nominative, coordinated with the nominative preceding them. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi 'Abla read all three in the accusative, meaning: and He created the grain. They permitted that "al-rayhan" be in the nominative or the accusative with an omitted modifier, meaning: and the possessor of the rayhan, omitting the modifier and putting the modifier-of-it in its place. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and al-Asma'i from Abu 'Amr read "wa-r-rayhani" in the genitive, and the meaning is: the grain that has husks, which is the fodder of beasts, and the rayhan, which is the food of people. The inclusion of the fragrant in the genitive reading is far-fetched. "Rayhan" is from the roots with a waw. Abu 'Ali permitted that it be a noun used in place of a verbal noun, and that it be a verbal noun of the pattern fa'lan, like al-labban. The waw was changed to a ya', just as they changed the ya' to a waw in ashawa. Or it is an irregular verbal noun from a defective root, as the irregular forms bununah and buynunah occur. Its original form is rayawhan; the waw was changed to a ya' and assimilated into the ya', becoming rayyhan, then the middle radical of the word was deleted, as they said: mayt and hayn.

When God, exalted is He, enumerated His blessings, He addressed the two weighty ones with His saying: ﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 32]. That is: His blessings are many and cannot be counted, so which of them will you deny? That is, one whose blessings are these cannot deny them. This address was to the two weighty ones, because both are included among the creatures according to the most correct opinions. This is also in keeping with His saying: ﴿He created man﴾ and ﴿and He created the jinn﴾, and with His saying: ﴿We will attend to you, O two weighty ones﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 31]. He who made it an address to males and females of the children of Adam has gone too far. Even further is the saying of one who said: it is an address in the manner of His saying: ﴿Cast into Hell﴾ [Qaf: 24], and "O my guard, strike his neck," meaning that it is an address to one person in the form of two. Then "fa-bi-ayyi" is tanwin in the whole surah, as if the genitive complement were omitted from it, and "ala'i rabbikuma" was substituted for it as a substitute of a definite from an indefinite. "Ala'" was previously stated in al-A'raf to mean blessings, its singular forms being ilyun, alan, ilan and alyun.

﴿He created man﴾: when He mentioned the greater world of the heaven and earth, and what He brought into existence in them of blessings, He mentioned the origin of the one for whom these blessings were created. "Al-insan" is Adam, and this is the view of the majority. It was said: it is the genus, and that was permissible because their father was created from clay. If by "al-insan" Adam is meant, then he passed through different stages, due to the transformation of his origin: he was first dust, then clay, then black mud molded, then dry clay. So it was appropriate that his creation be attributed to each of these. "Al-jann" is the father of the jinn, and he is Iblis, according to al-Hasan. Mujahid said: he is the father of the jinn, and not Iblis. It was said: "al-jann" is a generic noun. "Al-marij" is what is mixed of yellow, red and green, or the flame, or the pure, or the redness at the edge of the fire, or what is mixed with blackness, or what moves without smoke: these are opinions. ("Min") in the first is for the starting point of the end, and the second ("min nar") is partitive. It was said it is for explanation. The repetition in these refrains is for emphasis, alerting and stirring, and it appears in several places in the Qur'an. Some people, including Ibn Qutaybah, went to the view that this repetition is only for the variety of blessings, so He repeated the reminder (al-tawqif) for each one of them.

Al-Jumhur read "rabbu" and "rabbu" in the nominative, meaning: He is Lord. Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi 'Abla read it in the genitive as a substitute for "rabbikuma." He used the dual for the genitive complement because they are the two rising-places of summer and winter and their two setting-places, said Mujahid. It was said: the two rising-places of the sun and the moon and their two setting-places. From Ibn Abbas: the sun has a rising-place in summer that is high, and a rising-place in winter that is low, moving between them, rising and descending. He concluded.
