From Ibn Abi Ishaq also: "wa-nahisun" with the three vowels on the ha' by choice. Hanzalah ibn Nu'man: "wa-nahisin" with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the sin. Al-Hasan and Isma'il: "wa-nuhusin" with two dammas and a kasra. Zayd ibn 'Ali read: "nursilu" with the nun, "'alaykuma shuwazan" in the accusative, and "min narin wa-nuhasan" in the accusative, coordinated with "shuwazan." Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: al-nuhas is smoke. And it is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid that it is the well-known brass (al-sufr). The meaning is: he overcomes the jinn and humankind, that is, you two are in the state of one upon whom this is sent, so he cannot resist what is sent upon him.

﴿When the sky is split open﴾: the response of "idha" is omitted, that is, how great the terror is; its splitting is its cleaving on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Then it becomes rose-red﴾: that is, reddened like the rose. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Salih said: it is of the colour of the rose-coloured horse, so the feminine is used because the sky is feminine. Qatadah said: it is now blue, and on that day redness will prevail over it like the colour of the rose, which is the well-known narcissus; al-Zajjaj said this, meaning like the colour of the rose. The poet said:

If I were a rose whose colour you loved, you would have loved me, but my Lord has marred me with my blackness.

Abu al-Jawza' said: a rose-coloured yellow. He said: Have you not heard the Arabs call horses "al-ward"? Al-Farra' said: he meant the colour of the rose-coloured horse, which in spring is toward yellow, in winter toward red, and in intense cold toward grey; so the changing colour of the sky is likened to the changing colour of a rose-coloured horse. This is the saying of al-Kalbi.

﴿Like oil dregs (kal-dihan)﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: a red hide (adim). From it is the saying of al-A'sha:

And a sleek, noble, swift horse, as if upon its flanks was dihan.

The poet said: like the varied dihan, because it changes colours. Al-Dahhak said: like pure dihan, plural of duhn, like qirt and qirat. It has been said: it turns red from the heat of Hell, and like oil in its melting and turning. It has been said: it is likened to dihan in its shine. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿kal-dihan﴾: like the oil of olive, as He said: ﴿like molten metal (al-muhl)﴾ [al-Kahf: 29], which is the lees of oil; it is the plural of duhn or the name of what is anointed with it, like "haram" and "idam." The poet said:

As if they were two water-skins of a hasty man, both full, when they were drawn with dihan.

'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read "wardatun" in the nominative, meaning: so there resulted a rose-red sky; this is from the kind of speech called tajrid, like His saying:

So if I remain, I will surely go on a raid toward the spoils, or a noble man will die.

Ended.

﴿So on that Day﴾: the tanwin in it is in place of the omitted clause, and the estimate is: "on the day when the sky is split open," and the governor of "yawma'idhin" is ﴿will not be asked﴾, and this indicates the negation of questioning; and other verses, such as ﴿Stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [al-Saffat: 24] and others, indicate that questioning occurs. Ikrimah and Qatadah said: these are stations in some of which questioning occurs. Ibn 'Abbas said: wherever questioning is mentioned, it is a questioning of rebuke and establishing the fact, and wherever it is negated, it is a pure inquiry about the sin; and Allah knows best everything. Qatadah also said: there was questioning, then the mouths were sealed and the hands and feet spoke of what they used to do. Abu al-'Aliyah and Qatadah said: no one other than the criminal is asked about the sin of the criminal. Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read "wa-la jann" with a hamzah, to avoid the meeting of two sukun, though their meeting is within its rule. Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman read "bi-simaihim"; al-Jumhur read ﴿bi-simahum﴾. The marks of the criminals: blackness of faces and blueness of eyes, said al-Hasan; it is possible that it is other than this of disfigurements, such as blindness, muteness and deafness.

﴿They will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: he is seized by his forelock and his two feet, and he is trampled, and gathered like firewood, and thrown thus into the Fire. Al-Dahhak said: they are gathered together in a chain from behind their backs. It has been said: the angels drag them, sometimes seizing by the forelocks and sometimes by the feet. It has been said: some are dragged by the forelock and some are dragged by the foot. "Yu'khadhu" is transitive to an object by itself, and this agent and object have been omitted, and the prepositional phrase has taken the place of the subject, implying the sense of what is transitive by "bi," that is: "so they are dragged by the forelocks and the feet." The alif-lam in both, according to the Kufans, is a substitute for the pronoun, that is, "by their forelocks and their feet"; and according to the Basrans, the pronoun is omitted, that is, "by the forelocks and the feet of them."

﴿This is Hell﴾: that is, it is said to them in a manner of rebuke and reproach.

﴿They will circulate between it﴾: that is, they will go back and forth between its fire and what boils in it of its liquid torment. Qatadah said: the scalding water has been boiling since God created Hell, and "an" means the extreme of heat and ripeness; so they are punished, alternating between them and the burning of the Fire and between drinking the scalding water. It has been said: when they cry out for help from the Fire, the scalding water is made their relief. It has been said: they are plunged into a valley in Hell where the pus of the people of the Fire gathers, so their joints are dislocated, then they come out of it, and God has created for them a new creation. 'Ali and al-Sulami read "yutafuna"; al-A'mash, Talhah and Ibn Miqsam read "yutawwifuna" with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the ta', and a kasra on the waw, doubled. It was also read "yattawwafuna," meaning "yatatawwafuna." The majority read "yatufuna," the imperfect of tafa.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And for one who fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. Ibn al-Zubayr said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr.

﴿Maqama rabbihi﴾ is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it may be read as a genitive construction with the subject: the standing of his Lord over him. This is narrated from Mujahid, who said that it comes from His words: ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul with what it has earned...?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33], meaning the Guardian, the Watcher, so the servant is mindful of this and does not dare to disobey. It has also been said that the genitive relation can be formed by even the slightest connection, so the meaning is that he fears his station where the servants stand for reckoning, from His words: ﴿The Day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6]. In this construction there is an indication of the severity of that standing. It has also been said that maqam is inserted (muqhamm, an extra word), and the meaning is: "And for whoever fears his Lord," just as you say, "I fear the side of so-and-so," meaning so-and-so himself. The apparent sense is that for each one of those who fear there are ﴿two gardens﴾. It has been said that one of them is his dwelling, and the other is for his wives and servants. Muqatil said: the Garden of Eden and the Garden of Delight. It has also been said that they are two abodes, he moves from one to the other, so that the causes of his pleasure are abundant and the fruits of his honour appear. It has also been said that they are for the fearful in general, and the address is to the two species (al-thaqalan), jinn and mankind: one garden for the fearful among the jinn, and one garden for the fearful among mankind. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: a garden of gold for the foremost (al-sabiqun), and a garden of silver for the followers (al-tabi'un). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible to say: one garden for performing acts of obedience, and one garden for abstaining from sins, since legal obligation revolves around these two. And it may be said: one garden in which one spends the night, and another added to it as a favour, in accordance with His words: ﴿and more﴾ [Yunus: 26]. He singled out ﴿afnan﴾ for mention. It is the plural of fann, and it means the branches that spread out from the boughs of the tree, because they are the ones that bear leaves and fruit, from them the shade extends, and from them the fruits are gathered. It has also been said that afnan is the plural of fann, meaning the kinds and varieties of blessings. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The first view was said to be close to it by Mujahid and 'Ikrimah, and it is the preferable one, because the pattern af'al occurs with fa'al more often than with fa'l (with a sukun on the 'ayn), and fann is pluralised as funun.

﴿In them are two springs flowing﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are two springs, like the worldly one multiplied many times over. He also said: they flow with increase and honour upon the people of Paradise. Al-Hasan said: they flow with pure water: one of them is Tasnim, and the other is Salsabil. Ibn 'Atiyya said: one of them is of water, and the other is of wine. It has also been said: they flow in the heights and the lowlands from a mountain of musk.

﴿Two kinds﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: there is no tree in this world, sweet or bitter, but it is in Paradise, (p-197) even the colocynth tree, except that it is sweet. End of quotation. The meaning of zawjan (two kinds) is: fresh and dry, neither of them falling short of the other in goodness and pleasure. It has also been said: two sorts, one of which is well known and the other is strange. The separation between His words ﴿possessing branches﴾ and His words ﴿in them of every fruit﴾ is made by His words ﴿in them two springs flowing﴾. The branches are upon them the fruits, because one who enters a garden does not come except to enjoy its pleasure by looking at the greenness of the trees and the flowing of the rivers, and afterwards he begins to gather the fruits to eat.

﴿Reclining﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from His words ﴿and for whoever fears﴾. It is taken as plural in agreement with the meaning of man (whoever). It has also been said that the governing verb is omitted, meaning: they enjoy themselves, reclining. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the accusative in the sense of praise, and reclining is one of the attributes of one who lives in luxury, indicating physical health and a free heart. The meaning is: reclining in their dwellings ﴿upon couches﴾ [al-Rahman: 54]. The majority read furush (couches) with two dammas; Abu Haywa read it with a sukun on the ra'. In a hadith: "It was said to the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ: 'These linings are of brocade; what are the outer layers?' He said: 'They are of light, shining.'" If this is authentic, it is not permissible to explain it by anything else. It has also been said: they are of sundus (fine silk). Al-Hasan and al-Farra' said: the linings (batai') are the outer layers (zahai'r). It was narrated from Qatada. Al-Farra' said: the lining may be the outer layer and the outer layer the lining, because each of them may be the face, and the Arabs say: "This is the face of the sky" and "This is the belly of the sky."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 55, verse 31–53 (part 1 of 2):

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿We will attend to you, O two burdens (al-thaqalan)﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through; you will not pass through except with authority﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ ﴿There will be sent against you a flame of fire and molten brass, and you will not be victorious﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ ﴿And when the sky is split open and becomes rose-red like oil dregs﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ ﴿So on that Day, neither man nor jinn will be asked about his sin﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks, and they will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ ﴿This is Hell, which the criminals used to deny﴾ ﴿They will circulate between it and scalding, boiling water﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ ﴿And for one who fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ ﴿Both having branches﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ ﴿Within them are two flowing springs﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ ﴿Within them of every fruit are two kinds﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ ﴿Reclining on beds whose linings are of brocade﴾ [al-Rahman: 54].

When He, exalted, mentioned the blessings He had bestowed through the teaching of knowledge, the creation of man, the heaven and the earth, what He placed in them, and the perishing of what is upon the earth, He mentioned what pertains to the states of the Hereafter and the recompense, and said: ﴿We will attend to you﴾: that is, We will look into your affairs on the Day of Resurrection, not that He, exalted, had any preoccupation from which He would then become free. The speech of the Arabs proceeds on this line, that the meaning is: He will intend your reckoning. It is a metaphor from the saying of a man to one he threatens: "I will be free for you" (sa-afraghu laka), meaning: I will devote myself to bringing you down, free from everything that preoccupies me from it, so that I have no other occupation, and the intended meaning is to concentrate on taking vengeance upon him. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is possible that the threat is of a punishment in this world, but the first is clearer." Ended. He means: that this would be on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that it means the world will come to an end and its final stage will be reached, and at that point the affairs of creation which He referred to in His saying: ﴿Every day He is in a matter﴾ [al-Rahman: 29] will end, so there will remain only one affair, which is your recompense; so He made that a leisure for them by way of figure of speech." Ended.

What the linguists of the language hold is that faragha (to be free) is used when the occupation that a person was engaged in is over; therefore his saying required interpretation. It has been said that faragha may mean qasada (to intend) and ihtamma (to be concerned), and evidence for this is what Ibn al-Anbari cited from Jarir:

Now, indeed, I have turned (faraghtu) to Numayr, so this is the time when I was a torment to them.

That is: I intended. And al-Nahhas recited:

I turned (faraghtu) to the shackled slave in the fetters.

In a hadith: "Your Lord has become free (faraga) of four [matters]," and in it: "I will surely turn (la-atafarraghanna) to you, O wicked one," said to the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, at the 'Aqabah of Iram on the day of its pledge: that is, I will surely intend to nullify your affair. This is transmitted from al-Khalil, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'. Al-Jumhur read sa-nafrughu with the nun of majesty and a damma on the ra', from faragha with a fatha on the ra', which is the dialect of the Hijaz. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Haywah and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with the ya' of the third person. Qatadah and al-A'raj read it with the nun and a fatha on the ra', the imperfect of faragha with a kasra, which is a Tamimi dialect. Abu al-Sammal and 'Isa read it with a kasra on the nun and a fatha on the ra'. Abu Hatim said: it is the dialect of Lower Mudar. Al-A'mash and Abu Haywah in a variant from them, and Ibn Abi 'Abla and al-Za'faranani read it with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the ra', in the passive. 'Isa also read it with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the ra'. Al-A'raj also read it with a fatha on the ya' and the ra', and this is the transmission of Yunus, al-Ju'fi and 'Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr.

Al-thaqalan: the humankind and the jinn. They were so named because they are two heavy ones upon the face of the earth, or because they are burdened with sins, or because of the heaviness of mankind. The jinn were called a "thaqal" because of their proximity to humankind, and the thaqal is a great matter. In a hadith: "I am leaving among you the two thaqalan: the Book of Allah and my 'itrah," they were so named for their greatness and nobility.

The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿O assembly﴾ and what follows is an address from God to them on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿the Day of Calling-out﴾ [Ghafir: 32]. It has been said: it is said to them at that time. Al-Dahhak said: they flee to the regions of the earth because of the terror they see, but they find the angels have surrounded the earth, so they return from where they came, and at that time it is said to them. It has been said: it is an address in this world, and the meaning is: if you are able to flee from death. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿if you are able﴾ with your minds and your thinking, ﴿to pass through﴾, so that you know the knowledge of ﴿the regions﴾, that is, the directions of ﴿the heavens and the earth﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind﴾ serves as an explanation of His saying ﴿O two burdens﴾; ﴿if you are able﴾ to flee from My decree and to go out from My dominion, from My heaven and My earth, then do so; then He said: you will not be able to pass through ﴿except with authority﴾, meaning: with power, compulsion and dominance, and how could you have that; similar to it is: ﴿And you cannot escape in the earth or in the heaven﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 22]. Ended.

﴿Then pass through﴾: an imperative of incapacitation. Qatadah said: authority here means dominion, and they have no dominion. Al-Dahhak also said: while people are in their markets, the sky will open and the angels will descend, and the jinn and humankind will flee, and the angels will surround them. Zayd ibn 'Ali read: "if you two are able" (in-ista'tuma), addressing the dual of the two burdens and taking into account the jinn and humankind; but the majority read in the plural addressing the group, "if you are able" (in-ista'tum), because each of them has many individuals under it, as in His saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9].

﴿A flame of fire will be sent against you﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: when they come out of their graves, a flame drives them to the place of gathering. Shuwaz means the blaze of fire. Mujahid said: the red flame that is cut off. Al-Dahhak said: the smoke that comes out of the flame. Al-Jumhur read shuwazun with a damma on the shin; 'Isa, Ibn Kathir and Shibl read it with a kasra. Al-Jumhur read ﴿wa-nuhasun﴾ in the nominative; Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it in the genitive; al-Kalbi, Talhah and Mujahid read it with a kasra on the nun of "nihas" and the sin. Ibn Jubayr read "wa-nahsun," as you say "a day of misfortune (yawm nahs)." 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakrah and Ibn Abi Ishaq also read it as "wa-nahussu" in the imperfect, its perfect being hassahu, meaning he killed him, that is, "and he feels the torment." From Ibn Abi Ishaq also: "wa-nahisun" with the three vowels on the ha' by choice. Hanzalah ibn Nu'man: "wa-nahisin" with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the sin. Al-Hasan and Isma'il: "wa-nuhusin" with two dammas and a kasra. Zayd ibn 'Ali read: "nursilu" with the nun, "'alaykuma shuwazan" in the accusative, and "min narin wa-nuhasan" in the accusative, coordinated with "shuwazan." Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: al-nuhas is smoke. And it is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid that it is the well-known brass (al-sufr). The meaning is: he overcomes the jinn and humankind, that is, you two are in the state of one upon whom this is sent, so he cannot resist what is sent upon him.

﴿When the sky is split open﴾: the response of "idha" is omitted, that is, how great the terror is; its splitting is its cleaving on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Then it becomes rose-red﴾: that is, reddened like the rose. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Salih said: it is of the colour of the rose-coloured horse, so the feminine is used because the sky is feminine. Qatadah said: it is now blue, and on that day redness will prevail over it like the colour of the rose, which is the well-known narcissus; al-Zajjaj said this, meaning like the colour of the rose. The poet said:

If I were a rose whose colour you loved, you would have loved me, but my Lord has marred me with my blackness.

Abu al-Jawza' said: a rose-coloured yellow. He said: Have you not heard the Arabs call horses "al-ward"? Al-Farra' said: he meant the colour of the rose-coloured horse, which in spring is toward yellow, in winter toward red, and in intense cold toward grey; so the changing colour of the sky is likened to the changing colour of a rose-coloured horse. This is the saying of al-Kalbi.

﴿Like oil dregs (kal-dihan)﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: a red hide (adim). From it is the saying of al-A'sha:

And a sleek, noble, swift horse, as if upon its flanks was dihan.

The poet said: like the varied dihan, because it changes colours. Al-Dahhak said: like pure dihan, plural of duhn, like qirt and qirat. It has been said: it turns red from the heat of Hell, and like oil in its melting and turning. It has been said: it is likened to dihan in its shine. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿kal-dihan﴾: like the oil of olive, as He said: ﴿like molten metal (al-muhl)﴾ [al-Kahf: 29], which is the lees of oil; it is the plural of duhn or the name of what is anointed with it, like "haram" and "idam." The poet said:

As if they were two water-skins of a hasty man, both full, when they were drawn with dihan.

'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read "wardatun" in the nominative, meaning: so there resulted a rose-red sky; this is from the kind of speech called tajrid, like His saying:

So if I remain, I will surely go on a raid toward the spoils, or a noble man will die.

Ended.

﴿So on that Day﴾: the tanwin in it is in place of the omitted clause, and the estimate is: "on the day when the sky is split open," and the governor of "yawma'idhin" is ﴿will not be asked﴾, and this indicates the negation of questioning; and other verses, such as ﴿Stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [al-Saffat: 24] and others, indicate that questioning occurs. Ikrimah and Qatadah said: these are stations in some of which questioning occurs. Ibn 'Abbas said: wherever questioning is mentioned, it is a questioning of rebuke and establishing the fact, and wherever it is negated, it is a pure inquiry about the sin; and Allah knows best everything. Qatadah also said: there was questioning, then the mouths were sealed and the hands and feet spoke of what they used to do. Abu al-'Aliyah and Qatadah said: no one other than the criminal is asked about the sin of the criminal. Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read "wa-la jann" with a hamzah, to avoid the meeting of two sukun, though their meeting is within its rule. Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman read "bi-simaihim"; al-Jumhur read ﴿bi-simahum﴾. The marks of the criminals: blackness of faces and blueness of eyes, said al-Hasan; it is possible that it is other than this of disfigurements, such as blindness, muteness and deafness.

﴿They will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: he is seized by his forelock and his two feet, and he is trampled, and gathered like firewood, and thrown thus into the Fire. Al-Dahhak said: they are gathered together in a chain from behind their backs. It has been said: the angels drag them, sometimes seizing by the forelocks and sometimes by the feet. It has been said: some are dragged by the forelock and some are dragged by the foot. "Yu'khadhu" is transitive to an object by itself, and this agent and object have been omitted, and the prepositional phrase has taken the place of the subject, implying the sense of what is transitive by "bi," that is: "so they are dragged by the forelocks and the feet." The alif-lam in both, according to the Kufans, is a substitute for the pronoun, that is, "by their forelocks and their feet"; and according to the Basrans, the pronoun is omitted, that is, "by the forelocks and the feet of them."

﴿This is Hell﴾: that is, it is said to them in a manner of rebuke and reproach.

﴿They will circulate between it﴾: that is, they will go back and forth between its fire and what boils in it of its liquid torment. Qatadah said: the scalding water has been boiling since God created Hell, and "an" means the extreme of heat and ripeness; so they are punished, alternating between them and the burning of the Fire and between drinking the scalding water. It has been said: when they cry out for help from the Fire, the scalding water is made their relief. It has been said: they are plunged into a valley in Hell where the pus of the people of the Fire gathers, so their joints are dislocated, then they come out of it, and God has created for them a new creation. 'Ali and al-Sulami read "yutafuna"; al-A'mash, Talhah and Ibn Miqsam read "yutawwifuna" with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the ta', and a kasra on the waw, doubled. It was also read "yattawwafuna," meaning "yatatawwafuna." The majority read "yatufuna," the imperfect of tafa.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And for one who fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. Ibn al-Zubayr said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr.

﴿Maqama rabbihi﴾ is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it may be read as a genitive construction with the subject: the standing of his Lord over him. This is narrated from Mujahid, who said that it comes from His words: ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul with what it has earned...?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33], meaning the Guardian, the Watcher, so the servant is mindful of this and does not dare to disobey. It has also been said that the genitive relation can be formed by even the slightest connection, so the meaning is that he fears his station where the servants stand for reckoning, from His words: ﴿The Day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6]. In this construction there is an indication of the severity of that standing. It has also been said that maqam is inserted (muqhamm, an extra word), and the meaning is: "And for whoever fears his Lord," just as you say, "I fear the side of so-and-so," meaning so-and-so himself. The apparent sense is that for each one of those who fear there are ﴿two gardens﴾. It has been said that one of them is his dwelling, and the other is for his wives and servants. Muqatil said: the Garden of Eden and the Garden of Delight. It has also been said that they are two abodes, he moves from one to the other, so that the causes of his pleasure are abundant and the fruits of his honour appear. It has also been said that they are for the fearful in general, and the address is to the two species (al-thaqalan), jinn and mankind: one garden for the fearful among the jinn, and one garden for the fearful among mankind. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: a garden of gold for the foremost (al-sabiqun), and a garden of silver for the followers (al-tabi'un). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible to say: one garden for performing acts of obedience, and one garden for abstaining from sins, since legal obligation revolves around these two. And it may be said: one garden in which one spends the night, and another added to it as a favour, in accordance with His words: ﴿and more﴾ [Yunus: 26]. He singled out ﴿afnan﴾ for mention. It is the plural of fann, and it means the branches that spread out from the boughs of the tree, because they are the ones that bear leaves and fruit, from them the shade extends, and from them the fruits are gathered. It has also been said that afnan is the plural of fann, meaning the kinds and varieties of blessings. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The first view was said to be close to it by Mujahid and 'Ikrimah, and it is the preferable one, because the pattern af'al occurs with fa'al more often than with fa'l (with a sukun on the 'ayn), and fann is pluralised as funun.

﴿In them are two springs flowing﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are two springs, like the worldly one multiplied many times over. He also said: they flow with increase and honour upon the people of Paradise. Al-Hasan said: they flow with pure water: one of them is Tasnim, and the other is Salsabil. Ibn 'Atiyya said: one of them is of water, and the other is of wine. It has also been said: they flow in the heights and the lowlands from a mountain of musk.

﴿Two kinds﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: there is no tree in this world, sweet or bitter, but it is in Paradise, (p-197) even the colocynth tree, except that it is sweet. End of quotation. The meaning of zawjan (two kinds) is: fresh and dry, neither of them falling short of the other in goodness and pleasure. It has also been said: two sorts, one of which is well known and the other is strange. The separation between His words ﴿possessing branches﴾ and His words ﴿in them of every fruit﴾ is made by His words ﴿in them two springs flowing﴾. The branches are upon them the fruits, because one who enters a garden does not come except to enjoy its pleasure by looking at the greenness of the trees and the flowing of the rivers, and afterwards he begins to gather the fruits to eat.

﴿Reclining﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from His words ﴿and for whoever fears﴾. It is taken as plural in agreement with the meaning of man (whoever). It has also been said that the governing verb is omitted, meaning: they enjoy themselves, reclining. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the accusative in the sense of praise, and reclining is one of the attributes of one who lives in luxury, indicating physical health and a free heart. The meaning is: reclining in their dwellings ﴿upon couches﴾ [al-Rahman: 54]. The majority read furush (couches) with two dammas; Abu Haywa read it with a sukun on the ra'. In a hadith: "It was said to the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ: 'These linings are of brocade; what are the outer layers?' He said: 'They are of light, shining.'" If this is authentic, it is not permissible to explain it by anything else. It has also been said: they are of sundus (fine silk). Al-Hasan and al-Farra' said: the linings (batai') are the outer layers (zahai'r). It was narrated from Qatada. Al-Farra' said: the lining may be the outer layer and the outer layer the lining, because each of them may be the face, and the Arabs say: "This is the face of the sky" and "This is the belly of the sky."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is within reach.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Therein are those restraining their gaze, whom no man or jinn has touched before them.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿As if they were rubies and coral.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿And beneath them are two other gardens.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Dark green.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Therein are two gushing springs.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Therein are fruit, palm trees and pomegranates.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Therein are good and beautiful [women].﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Maidens restrained in pavilions.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Whom no man or jinn has touched before them.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Reclining on green cushions and beautiful rich carpets.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas said: [They pick it] standing, sitting and lying down; neither distance nor thorns prevent their hand from reaching it.

'Isa [ibn 'Umar] recited ﴿wajna﴾ with a fatha on the jim and a kasra on the nun, as if he inclined the nun (imalah, pronouncing a vowel toward a following sound), even though the alif had been dropped in pronunciation, just as Abu 'Amr inclined in ﴿hatta nara Allah﴾. It was also read as ﴿wajni﴾ with a kasra on the jim. [Note: the Arabic names two qira'ah (recitation variants) here.]

The pronoun in ﴿fihinna﴾ refers to the gardens (al-jinan), which is indicated by "two gardens," since each individual is given two gardens, so it is correct to say that they are many gardens. Even if "the two gardens" is meant literally as the dual, and each category of jinn and humans has one garden, the pronoun refers to what the garden contains of assembly places, palaces and dwellings. It was also said that it refers to the couches (furush), meaning that therein they are prepared for enjoyment; this is a good view and close in its derivation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Therein" refers to these enumerated favours, namely the two gardens, the two springs, the fruit and the harvest. End of quote; but this is far-fetched. Al-Farra' said: Every place in the garden is a garden, which is why it says ﴿fihinna﴾. The word ﴿al-tarf﴾ (gaze) is originally a verbal noun, which is why it is singular. The apparent meaning is that they are the ones who restrict their eyes to their husbands, so they do not look at others. Ibn Zayd said: She says to her husband, "By the might of my Lord, I see nothing in Paradise more beautiful than you." It was also said that ﴿al-tarf﴾ is the gaze of others, meaning that they restrain the eyes of whoever looks at them from looking at anyone else.

﴿Lam yatmithhunna﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: No one has deflowered them before their husbands. It was also said: No one has had intercourse with them in any manner, whether by deflowering or otherwise; this is the view of 'Ikrimah. The pronoun in ﴿qablahum﴾ refers to whoever the pronoun in ﴿muttaki'in﴾ refers to. The majority read ﴿yatmithhunna﴾ with a kasra on the mim in both places. Talhah, 'Isa, the companions of 'Abd Allah and 'Ali read it with a damma. Some read with a damma on the first and a kasra on the second, some with the reverse, some with the option of either, and al-Jahdari read it with a fatha on the mim in both places. The negation of their being touched by humans is clear. As for jinn, Mujahid and al-Hasan said: The wives of humans may be had intercourse with by their husbands when the husband does not mention God Most High, so here the verse negates all who have intercourse. Damrah ibn Habib said: The jinn in Paradise have with them restrained-gazed women from their own kind of jinn, so the verse negates deflowering by both human and jinn women. Qatadah said: ﴿Ka'annahunna﴾ [as if they were] means in the clearness of rubies and the redness of coral; if you inserted a thread into a ruby and looked at it, you would see it from behind. End of quote. In al-Tirmidhi: "The woman among the women of Paradise, the whiteness of her shin will be seen from behind seventy garments, and its marrow." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Rubies and coral are among the things by whose beauty one is delighted, so they were compared with what is fitting for comparison: the ruby in its smoothness and its translucence, and coral in its smoothness and the beauty of its appearance. In this manner of reflection the Arabs named women after them, such as Durrah bint Abi Lahab and Marjanah, mother of Sa'id. End of quote.

﴿Hal jaza'u al-ihsan﴾ [Is the reward of goodness]: in action; ﴿illa al-ihsan﴾ [anything but goodness]: in reward. It was also said: Is the reward of monotheism anything but Paradise? Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿illa al-hisan﴾ [anything but the beautiful ones], meaning by the hisan the wide-eyed maidens (al-hur al-'in).

﴿Wa min dunihima﴾ [And beneath them]: that is, beneath those two gardens in rank and value, ﴿two gardens﴾ are for the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin). The first two are for the foremost (al-sabiqun); this was said by Ibn Zayd and most scholars. Al-Hasan said: The first two are for the foremost, and the latter two for the followers. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿Wa min dunihima﴾ in nearness is for the favoured ones, and the two mentioned later are better than the two mentioned first. This is shown by the fact that He described these two as having gushing springs, and those two only as having flowing streams; and these two as dark green, which is a source of delight, and those two as having branches, and every garden has branches. Al-Zamakhshari preferred this view and said: For the near ones there are two gardens, and beneath them, for the companions of the right, are two gardens dark green from intense greenness. Others preferred the first view, citing the mention of flowing in the two springs (that they gush, not merely flow), and His saying about them: ﴿of every fruit﴾ [55:52], and about the latter two: ﴿therein are fruit﴾; and [the mention of] reclining on what has brocade for its linings, which is the furnishings, while for the latter two the reclining is on the rafraf, which is the edge of the tent; and furnishings prepared for reclining are better. The 'abqari is embroidery and brocade, which is higher than it. What is compared to rubies and coral is better in description than "good and beautiful." The apparent meaning of gushing is with water. Ibn Jubayr said: With musk, ambergris and camphor in the houses of the people of Paradise, as the rain sprinkles. It is also reported from him: with various kinds of fruit and water.

﴿Wa nakhlun wa rummanun﴾ [palm trees and pomegranates]: he connected them with "fruit," and the conjunction implies that they are not included within fruit; this was said by some. Yunus ibn Habib and others said: He repeated them, though they are among the best fruits, to honour them and to point to them, as He said: ﴿and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [2:98]. It was also said: Because the date palm's fruit is both fruit and food, and the pomegranate is fruit and medicine, so they were not reserved purely for fruit-eating.

﴿Fihinna khayratun﴾: the plural of khayrah, an adjective formed on the pattern fa'lah from khayr (good), just as they formed from sharr (evil) the word sharrah. It was also said it is a lightened form of khayyirah, and Bakr ibn Habib, Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi and Ibn Miqsam read it so, meaning with a shadda on the ya'. It is reported from Abu 'Amr with a fatha on the ya', as if it were the plural of khayirah, pluralized on the pattern fa'lah. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) explained this to Umm Salamah, saying: "Those who are good in character, beautiful in faces."

﴿Hur maqsurat﴾ [wide-eyed maidens restrained]: that is, they are confined to their places. Women are praised for this, since their staying in the houses indicates their chastity, as Qays ibn al-Aslat said:

"She is lax toward her neighbours, so they visit her; and she is heedless of her own dwellings, so she is excused."

Al-Hasan said: They do not wander about in the streets. The tents of Paradise are houses of pearls. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: They are a hollow pearl. 'Abd Allah related it from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding ﴿whom no man or jinn has touched before them﴾: that is, before the companions of the two gardens, and the mention of the two gardens indicated them.

﴿Muttaki'in﴾ [reclining]: al-Zamakhshari said: It is in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas).

﴿'Ala rafraf﴾ [on green cushions]: Ibn 'Abbas and others said: the surplus of the sitting place and the carpets. Ibn Jubayr said: the gardens of Paradise, from raffa al-bayt (the house was adorned and became pleasant). Ibn 'Uyaynah said: the zarabi (cushions). Al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: the armrests (al-marafiq). Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah read al-majalis (the sitting places). As for 'abqari, al-Hasan said: fine carpets in which there are images and other things made in 'Abqar. Ibn 'Abbas said: the zarabi. Mujahid said: thick brocade. Ibn Zayd said: the tanafis (fine rugs). Al-Farra' said: the thick ones of them. The majority read ﴿'ala rafrafin﴾, and it is described with a plural because it is a noun of genus, whose single unit is rafrafah; a noun of genus may have its adjective in the singular or the plural, as in His saying: ﴿and the palm trees, tall (baasiqat)﴾ [50:10]. Its plural is made beautiful here by its matching with hisan, which is the rhyme-ending (fasilah). The author of al-Lawami' said: 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Nasr ibn 'Asim, al-Jahdari, Malik ibn Dinar, Ibn Muhaysin and Zuhayr al-'Uqayli and others read rafarif, a plural that does not take tanwin; khudr with a sukun on the dad; and 'abaqiriyy with a kasra on the qaf and a shadda on the ya'. It is also reported from them: a damma on the dad; and also a fatha on the qaf. He said: As for the prohibition of tanwin on 'abaqiriyy, which denotes garments ascribed to 'Abqar, a place from which garments were imported in ancient times, if it is not because of its proximity, then there is no reason for the ya' of nisba to prevent the use of tanwin except in poetic necessity. End of quote. Ibn Khalawayh said: 'ala rafarif khudr and 'abaqiriyy were read by the Prophet (ﷺ), al-Jahdari and Ibn Muhaysin. It is related from those we have mentioned: 'ala rafarif khudr and 'abaqiriyy with tanwin, and likewise it is related from Malik ibn Dinar. Abu Muhammad al-Marwazi, who was a grammarian, read: 'ala rafarif khidar, meaning on the pattern fi'al. The author of al-Kamil said: "Rafarif" is a plural, from Ibn Musarrif, Ibn Miqsam and Ibn Muhaysin; it was chosen by Shibl, Abu Haywah, al-Jahdari and al-Za'farani, and it is the preferred reading because of His saying ﴿khudr﴾. And 'abaqiriyy in the plural, with a kasra on the qaf without tanwin, was read by Ibn Miqsam and Ibn Muhaysin, and tanwin is also reported from them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Zuhayr al-'Uqayli read rafarif with the plural and with tanwin; and from him: 'abaqara with a fatha on the qaf and ya', on the basis that the name of the place is 'abaqar with a fatha on the qaf; but the correct form for the name of the place is 'abqar. End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said, and Abu Hatim related: 'abaqara with a fatha on the qaf and without tanwin, and this has no basis for its soundness. End of quote. It may be said: when he made rafarif without tanwin, he made 'abaqiri parallel to it, just as something that does not take tanwin may be given tanwin for the sake of parallelism, and something that takes tanwin may be denied it for the sake of parallelism. Ibn Hurmuz read khudr with a damma on the dad. The author of al-Lawami' said: This is a rare dialect. End of quote. From it is the saying of Tarafah:

"O young men in our gathering, strip off from it the bay and the chestnut."

Another said:

"I have not allied myself with a weakling, nor with the lowly, nor with the base of heart, on the day of terror."

So shuqr is the plural of ashqar (chestnut), and kusuf is the plural of aksaf (base).

The majority read ﴿Dhi al-Jalal﴾ as an adjective of "your Lord." Ibn 'Amir and the people of Syria read dhu as an adjective of the name (al-ism). In the reading of Abu 'Abd Allah and Ubayy it is dhi al-jalal, as in their reading in the first place, and the meaning here of "the name" is the named (al-musamma). It was also said: the name is an extra word (ism muqham), like "the face" in ﴿and there remains the face of your Lord﴾ [55:27]. This is indicated by the attribution of ﴿tabaraka﴾ (blessed be) to other than the name in several places, as in His saying: ﴿So blessed be God, the best of creators﴾ [23:14], ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills﴾ [25:10], ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾ [67:1]. The attribution to the name is also valid, since it means elevation; if the name is elevated, what then of the named? When He concluded the favours of this world with His saying: ﴿And there remains the face of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾ [55:27], He concluded the favours of the Hereafter with His saying: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour.﴾ There, mention of permanence and everlastingness fitted Him, since He had mentioned the perishing of the world; and here, mention of what is derived from barakah (blessing, which is growth and increase) fits, since this comes after what He had bestowed as a favour upon the believers, and what He gave them in the abode of His honour of good and its increase and its perpetuity. And "O Possessor of Majesty and Honour" is among the attributes by which God is called upon, as the hadith says. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Persist in calling upon Him as Possessor of Majesty and Honour."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is within reach.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Therein are those restraining their gaze, whom no man or jinn has touched before them.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿As if they were rubies and coral.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿And beneath them are two other gardens.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Dark green.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Therein are two gushing springs.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Therein are fruit, palm trees and pomegranates.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Therein are good and beautiful [women].﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Maidens restrained in pavilions.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Whom no man or jinn has touched before them.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Reclining on green cushions and beautiful rich carpets.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas said: [They pick it] standing, sitting and lying down; neither distance nor thorns prevent their hand from reaching it.

'Isa [ibn 'Umar] recited ﴿wajna﴾ with a fatha on the jim and a kasra on the nun, as if he inclined the nun (imalah, pronouncing a vowel toward a following sound), even though the alif had been dropped in pronunciation, just as Abu 'Amr inclined in ﴿hatta nara Allah﴾. It was also read as ﴿wajni﴾ with a kasra on the jim. [Note: the Arabic names two qira'ah (recitation variants) here.]

The pronoun in ﴿fihinna﴾ refers to the gardens (al-jinan), which is indicated by "two gardens," since each individual is given two gardens, so it is correct to say that they are many gardens. Even if "the two gardens" is meant literally as the dual, and each category of jinn and humans has one garden, the pronoun refers to what the garden contains of assembly places, palaces and dwellings. It was also said that it refers to the couches (furush), meaning that therein they are prepared for enjoyment; this is a good view and close in its derivation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Therein" refers to these enumerated favours, namely the two gardens, the two springs, the fruit and the harvest. End of quote; but this is far-fetched. Al-Farra' said: Every place in the garden is a garden, which is why it says ﴿fihinna﴾. The word ﴿al-tarf﴾ (gaze) is originally a verbal noun, which is why it is singular. The apparent meaning is that they are the ones who restrict their eyes to their husbands, so they do not look at others. Ibn Zayd said: She says to her husband, "By the might of my Lord, I see nothing in Paradise more beautiful than you." It was also said that ﴿al-tarf﴾ is the gaze of others, meaning that they restrain the eyes of whoever looks at them from looking at anyone else.

﴿Lam yatmithhunna﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: No one has deflowered them before their husbands. It was also said: No one has had intercourse with them in any manner, whether by deflowering or otherwise; this is the view of 'Ikrimah. The pronoun in ﴿qablahum﴾ refers to whoever the pronoun in ﴿muttaki'in﴾ refers to. The majority read ﴿yatmithhunna﴾ with a kasra on the mim in both places. 'Isa [ibn 'Umar] recited ﴿wajna﴾ with a fatha on the jim and a kasra on the nun, as if he inclined the nun (imalah, pronouncing a vowel toward a following sound), even though the alif had been dropped in pronunciation, just as Abu 'Amr inclined in ﴿hatta nara Allah﴾. It was also read as ﴿wajni﴾ with a kasra on the jim. [Note: the Arabic names two qira'ah (recitation variants) here.]

Even if "the two gardens" is meant literally as the dual, and each category of jinn and humans has one garden, the pronoun refers to what the garden contains of assembly places, palaces and dwellings. It was also said that it refers to the couches (furush), meaning that therein they are prepared for enjoyment; this is a good view and close in its derivation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Therein" refers to these enumerated favours, namely the two gardens, the two springs, the fruit and the harvest. End of quote; but this is far-fetched. Al-Farra' said: Every place in the garden is a garden, which is why it says ﴿fihinna﴾. The word ﴿al-tarf﴾ (gaze) is originally a verbal noun, which is why it is singular. The apparent meaning is that they are the ones who restrict their eyes to their husbands, so they do not look at others. Ibn Zayd said: She says to her husband, "By the might of my Lord, I see nothing in Paradise more beautiful than you." It was also said that ﴿al-tarf﴾ is the gaze of others, meaning that they restrain the eyes of whoever looks at them from looking at anyone else.

﴿Lam yatmithhunna﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: No one has deflowered them before their husbands. It was also said: No one has had intercourse with them in any manner, whether by deflowering or otherwise; this is the view of 'Ikrimah. The pronoun in ﴿qablahum﴾ refers to whoever the pronoun in ﴿muttaki'in﴾ refers to. The majority read ﴿yatmithhunna﴾ with a kasra on the mim in both places. Talhah, 'Isa, the companions of 'Abd Allah and 'Ali read it with a damma. Some read with a damma on the first and a kasra on the second, some with the reverse, some with the option of either, and al-Jahdari read it with a fatha on the mim in both places. The negation of their being touched by humans is clear. As for jinn, Mujahid and al-Hasan said: The wives of humans may be had intercourse with by their husbands when the husband does not mention God Most High, so here the verse negates all who have intercourse. Damrah ibn Habib said: The jinn in Paradise have with them restrained-gazed women from their own kind of jinn, so the verse negates deflowering by both human and jinn women. Qatadah said: ﴿Ka'annahunna﴾ [as if they were] means in the clearness of rubies and the redness of coral; if you inserted a thread into a ruby and looked at it, you would see it from behind. End of quote. In al-Tirmidhi: "The woman among the women of Paradise, the whiteness of her shin will be seen from behind seventy garments, and its marrow." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Rubies and coral are among the things by whose beauty one is delighted, so they were compared with what is fitting for comparison: the ruby in its smoothness and its translucence, and coral in its smoothness and the beauty of its appearance. In this manner of reflection the Arabs named women after them, such as Durrah bint Abi Lahab and Marjanah, mother of Sa'id. End of quote.

So shuqr is the plural of ashqar (chestnut), and kusuf is the plural of aksaf (base).

The majority read ﴿Dhi al-Jalal﴾ as an adjective of "your Lord." Ibn 'Amir and the people of Syria read dhu as an adjective of the name (al-ism). In the reading of Abu 'Abd Allah and Ubayy it is dhi al-jalal, as in their reading in the first place, and the meaning here of "the name" is the named (al-musamma). It was also said: the name is an extra word (ism muqham), like "the face" in ﴿and there remains the face of your Lord﴾ [55:27]. This is indicated by the attribution of ﴿tabaraka﴾ (blessed be) to other than the name in several places, as in His saying: ﴿So blessed be God, the best of creators﴾ [23:14], ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills﴾ [25:10], ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾ [67:1]. The attribution to the name is also valid, since it means elevation; if the name is elevated, what then of the named? When He concluded the favours of this world with His saying: ﴿And there remains the face of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾ [55:27], He concluded the favours of the Hereafter with His saying: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour.﴾ There, mention of permanence and everlastingness fitted Him, since He had mentioned the perishing of the world; and here, mention of what is derived from barakah (blessing, which is growth and increase) fits, since this comes after what He had bestowed as a favour upon the believers, and what He gave them in the abode of His honour of good and its increase and its perpetuity. And "O Possessor of Majesty and Honour" is among the attributes by which God is called upon, as the hadith says. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Persist in calling upon Him as Possessor of Majesty and Honour."

It was also said: No one has had intercourse with them in any manner, whether by deflowering or otherwise; this is the view of 'Ikrimah. Talhah, 'Isa, the companions of 'Abd Allah and 'Ali read it with a damma. Abu Muhammad al-Marwazi, who was a grammarian, read: 'ala rafarif khidar, meaning on the pattern fi'al. The author of al-Kamil said: "Rafarif" is a plural, from Ibn Musarrif, Ibn Miqsam and Ibn Muhaysin; it was chosen by Shibl, Abu Haywah, al-Jahdari and al-Za'farani, and it is the preferred reading because of His saying ﴿khudr﴾. And 'abaqiriyy in the plural, with a kasra on the qaf without tanwin, was read by Ibn Miqsam and Ibn Muhaysin, and tanwin is also reported from them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Zuhayr al-'Uqayli read rafarif with the plural and with tanwin; and from him: 'abaqara with a fatha on the qaf and ya', on the basis that the name of the place is 'abaqar with a fatha on the qaf; but the correct form for the name of the place is 'abqar. End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said, and Abu Hatim related: 'abaqara with a fatha on the qaf and without tanwin, and this has no basis for its soundness. End of quote. It may be said: when he made rafarif without tanwin, he made 'abaqiri parallel to it, just as something that does not take tanwin may be given tanwin for the sake of parallelism, and something that takes tanwin may be denied it for the sake of parallelism. Ibn Hurmuz read khudr with a damma on the dad. The author of al-Lawami' said: This is a rare dialect. End of quote. From it is the saying of Tarafah:

"O young men in our gathering, strip off from it the bay and the chestnut."

Another said:

"I have not allied myself with a weakling, nor with the lowly, nor with the base of heart, on the day of terror."

Ibn 'Abbas said: [They pick it] standing, sitting and lying down; neither distance nor thorns prevent their hand from reaching it.

It was also said that it refers to the couches (furush), meaning that therein they are prepared for enjoyment; this is a good view and close in its derivation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Therein" refers to these enumerated favours, namely the two gardens, the two springs, the fruit and the harvest. End of quote; but this is far-fetched. The apparent meaning is that they are the ones who restrict their eyes to their husbands, so they do not look at others. Ibn Zayd said: She says to her husband, "By the might of my Lord, I see nothing in Paradise more beautiful than you." It was also said that ﴿al-tarf﴾ is the gaze of others, meaning that they restrain the eyes of whoever looks at them from looking at anyone else.

It was also said: No one has had intercourse with them in any manner, whether by deflowering or otherwise; this is the view of 'Ikrimah. The pronoun in ﴿qablahum﴾ refers to whoever the pronoun in ﴿muttaki'in﴾ refers to. The majority read ﴿yatmithhunna﴾ with a kasra on the mim in both places. Talhah, 'Isa, the companions of 'Abd Allah and 'Ali read it with a damma. Some read with a damma on the first and a kasra on the second, some with the reverse, some with the option of either, and al-Jahdari read it with a fatha on the mim in both places. The negation of their being touched by humans is clear. As for jinn, Mujahid and al-Hasan said: The wives of humans may be had intercourse with by their husbands when the husband does not mention God Most High, so here the verse negates all who have intercourse. Damrah ibn Habib said: The jinn in Paradise have with them restrained-gazed women from their own kind of jinn, so the verse negates deflowering by both human and jinn women. Qatadah said: ﴿Ka'annahunna﴾ [as if they were] means in the clearness of rubies and the redness of coral; if you inserted a thread into a ruby and looked at it, you would see it from behind. "O young men in our gathering, strip off from it the bay and the chestnut."

Another said:

"I have not allied myself with a weakling, nor with the lowly, nor with the base of heart, on the day of terror."

So shuqr is the plural of ashqar (chestnut), and kusuf is the plural of aksaf (base).

Ibn 'Abbas said: [They pick it] standing, sitting and lying down; neither distance nor thorns prevent their hand from reaching it.

'Isa [ibn 'Umar] recited ﴿wajna﴾ with a fatha on the jim and a kasra on the nun, as if he inclined the nun (imalah, pronouncing a vowel toward a following sound), even though the alif had been dropped in pronunciation, just as Abu 'Amr inclined in ﴿hatta nara Allah﴾. It was also read as ﴿wajni﴾ with a kasra on the jim. [Note: the Arabic names two qira'ah (recitation variants) here.]

Even if "the two gardens" is meant literally as the dual, and each category of jinn and humans has one garden, the pronoun refers to what the garden contains of assembly places, palaces and dwellings. It was also said that it refers to the couches (furush), meaning that therein they are prepared for enjoyment; this is a good view and close in its derivation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Therein" refers to these enumerated favours, namely the two gardens, the two springs, the fruit and the harvest. End of quote; but this is far-fetched. Al-Farra' said: Every place in the garden is a garden, which is why it says ﴿fihinna﴾. The word ﴿al-tarf﴾ (gaze) is originally a verbal noun, which is why it is singular. The apparent meaning is that they are the ones who restrict their eyes to their husbands, so they do not look at others. Ibn Zayd said: She says to her husband, "By the might of my Lord, I see nothing in Paradise more beautiful than you." It was also said that ﴿al-tarf﴾ is the gaze of others, meaning that they restrain the eyes of whoever looks at them from looking at anyone else.

﴿Lam yatmithhunna﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: No one has deflowered them before their husbands. It was also said: No one has had intercourse with them in any manner, whether by deflowering or otherwise; this is the view of 'Ikrimah. The pronoun in ﴿qablahum﴾ refers to whoever the pronoun in ﴿muttaki'in﴾ refers to. The majority read ﴿yatmithhunna﴾ with a kasra on the mim in both places. Talhah, 'Isa, the companions of 'Abd Allah and 'Ali read it with a damma. Some read with a damma on the first and a kasra on the second, some with the reverse, some with the option of either, and al-Jahdari read it with a fatha on the mim in both places. The negation of their being touched by humans is clear. As for jinn, Mujahid and al-Hasan said: The wives of humans may be had intercourse with by their husbands when the husband does not mention God Most High, so here the verse negates all who have intercourse. Damrah ibn Habib said: The jinn in Paradise have with them restrained-gazed women from their own kind of jinn, so the verse negates deflowering by both human and jinn women. Qatadah said: ﴿Ka'annahunna﴾ [as if they were] means in the clearness of rubies and the redness of coral; if you inserted a thread into a ruby and looked at it, you would see it from behind. End of quote. In al-Tirmidhi: "The woman among the women of Paradise, the whiteness of her shin will be seen from behind seventy garments, and its marrow." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Rubies and coral are among the things by whose beauty one is delighted, so they were compared with what is fitting for comparison: the ruby in its smoothness and its translucence, and coral in its smoothness and the beauty of its appearance. In this manner of reflection the Arabs named women after them, such as Durrah bint Abi Lahab and Marjanah, mother of Sa'id. End of quote.

Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿illa al-hisan﴾ [anything but the beautiful ones], meaning by the hisan the wide-eyed maidens (al-hur al-'in).

﴿Wa min dunihima﴾ [And beneath them]: that is, beneath those two gardens in rank and value, ﴿two gardens﴾ are for the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin). The first two are for the foremost (al-sabiqun); this was said by Ibn Zayd and most scholars. Al-Hasan said: The first two are for the foremost, and the latter two for the followers. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿Wa min dunihima﴾ in nearness is for the favoured ones, and the two mentioned later are better than the two mentioned first. This is shown by the fact that He described these two as having gushing springs, and those two only as having flowing streams; and these two as dark green, which is a source of delight, and those two as having branches, and every garden has branches. Al-Zamakhshari preferred this view and said: For the near ones there are two gardens, and beneath them, for the companions of the right, are two gardens dark green from intense greenness. Others preferred the first view, citing the mention of flowing in the two springs (that they gush, not merely flow), and His saying about them: ﴿of every fruit﴾ [55:52], and about the latter two: ﴿therein are fruit﴾; and [the mention of] reclining on what has brocade for its linings, which is the furnishings, while for the latter two the reclining is on the rafraf, which is the edge of the tent; and furnishings prepared for reclining are better. The 'abqari is embroidery and brocade, which is higher than it. What is compared to rubies and coral is better in description than "good and beautiful." The apparent meaning of gushing is with water. Ibn Jubayr said: With musk, ambergris and camphor in the houses of the people of Paradise, as the rain sprinkles. It is also reported from him: with various kinds of fruit and water.

﴿Wa nakhlun wa rummanun﴾ [palm trees and pomegranates]: he connected them with "fruit," and the conjunction implies that they are not included within fruit; this was said by some. Yunus ibn Habib and others said: He repeated them, though they are among the best fruits, to honour them and to point to them, as He said: ﴿and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [2:98]. It was also said: Because the date palm's fruit is both fruit and food, and the pomegranate is fruit and medicine, so they were not reserved purely for fruit-eating.

﴿Fihinna khayratun﴾: the plural of khayrah, an adjective formed on the pattern fa'lah from khayr (good), just as they formed from sharr (evil) the word sharrah. It was also said it is a lightened form of khayyirah, and Bakr ibn Habib, Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi and Ibn Miqsam read it so, meaning with a shadda on the ya'. It is reported from Abu 'Amr with a fatha on the ya', as if it were the plural of khayirah, pluralized on the pattern fa'lah. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) explained this to Umm Salamah, saying: "Those who are good in character, beautiful in faces."

"She is lax toward her neighbours, so they visit her; and she is heedless of her own dwellings, so she is excused."

Ibn 'Abbas said: [They pick it] standing, sitting and lying down; neither distance nor thorns prevent their hand from reaching it.

It was also said that it refers to the couches (furush), meaning that therein they are prepared for enjoyment; this is a good view and close in its derivation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Therein" refers to these enumerated favours, namely the two gardens, the two springs, the fruit and the harvest. End of quote; but this is far-fetched. The apparent meaning is that they are the ones who restrict their eyes to their husbands, so they do not look at others. It was also said that ﴿al-tarf﴾ is the gaze of others, meaning that they restrain the eyes of whoever looks at them from looking at anyone else.

It was also said: No one has had intercourse with them in any manner, whether by deflowering or otherwise; this is the view of 'Ikrimah. Talhah, 'Isa, the companions of 'Abd Allah and 'Ali read it with a damma. Damrah ibn Habib said: The jinn in Paradise have with them restrained-gazed women from their own kind of jinn, so the verse negates deflowering by both human and jinn women. Qatadah said: ﴿Ka'annahunna﴾ [as if they were] means in the clearness of rubies and the redness of coral; if you inserted a thread into a ruby and looked at it, you would see it from behind. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Zuhayr al-'Uqayli read rafarif with the plural and with tanwin; and from him: 'abaqara with a fatha on the qaf and ya', on the basis that the name of the place is 'abaqar with a fatha on the qaf; but the correct form for the name of the place is 'abqar. "O young men in our gathering, strip off from it the bay and the chestnut."

Another said:

"I have not allied myself with a weakling, nor with the lowly, nor with the base of heart, on the day of terror."

So shuqr is the plural of ashqar (chestnut), and kusuf is the plural of aksaf (base).

The majority read ﴿Dhi al-Jalal﴾ as an adjective of "your Lord." Ibn 'Amir and the people of Syria read dhu as an adjective of the name (al-ism). In the reading of Abu 'Abd Allah and Ubayy it is dhi al-jalal, as in their reading in the first place, and the meaning here of "the name" is the named (al-musamma). It was also said: the name is an extra word (ism muqham), like "the face" in ﴿and there remains the face of your Lord﴾ [55:27]. This is indicated by the attribution of ﴿tabaraka﴾ (blessed be) to other than the name in several places, as in His saying: ﴿So blessed be God, the best of creators﴾ [23:14], ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills﴾ [25:10], ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾ [67:1]. The attribution to the name is also valid, since it means elevation; if the name is elevated, what then of the named? "O young men in our gathering, strip off from it the bay and the chestnut."

Another said:

"I have not allied myself with a weakling, nor with the lowly, nor with the base of heart, on the day of terror."

So shuqr is the plural of ashqar (chestnut), and kusuf is the plural of aksaf (base).

Ibn 'Abbas said: [They pick it] standing, sitting and lying down; neither distance nor thorns prevent their hand from reaching it.

'Isa [ibn 'Umar] recited ﴿wajna﴾ with a fatha on the jim and a kasra on the nun, as if he inclined the nun (imalah, pronouncing a vowel toward a following sound), even though the alif had been dropped in pronunciation, just as Abu 'Amr inclined in ﴿hatta nara Allah﴾. It was also read as ﴿wajni﴾ with a kasra on the jim. [Note: the Arabic names two qira'ah (recitation variants) here.]

Even if "the two gardens" is meant literally as the dual, and each category of jinn and humans has one garden, the pronoun refers to what the garden contains of assembly places, palaces and dwellings. It was also said that it refers to the couches (furush), meaning that therein they are prepared for enjoyment; this is a good view and close in its derivation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Therein" refers to these enumerated favours, namely the two gardens, the two springs, the fruit and the harvest. End of quote; but this is far-fetched. Al-Farra' said: Every place in the garden is a garden, which is why it says ﴿fihinna﴾. The word ﴿al-tarf﴾ (gaze) is originally a verbal noun, which is why it is singular. The apparent meaning is that they are the ones who restrict their eyes to their husbands, so they do not look at others. Ibn Zayd said: She says to her husband, "By the might of my Lord, I see nothing in Paradise more beautiful than you." It was also said that ﴿al-tarf﴾ is the gaze of others, meaning that they restrain the eyes of whoever looks at them from looking at anyone else.

﴿Lam yatmithhunna﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: No one has deflowered them before their husbands. It was also said: No one has had intercourse with them in any manner, whether by deflowering or otherwise; this is the view of 'Ikrimah. The pronoun in ﴿qablahum﴾ refers to whoever the pronoun in ﴿muttaki'in﴾ refers to. The majority read ﴿yatmithhunna﴾ with a kasra on the mim in both places. Talhah, 'Isa, the companions of 'Abd Allah and 'Ali read it with a damma. Some read with a damma on the first and a kasra on the second, some with the reverse, some with the option of either, and al-Jahdari read it with a fatha on the mim in both places. The negation of their being touched by humans is clear. As for jinn, Mujahid and al-Hasan said: The wives of humans may be had intercourse with by their husbands when the husband does not mention God Most High, so here the verse negates all who have intercourse. Damrah ibn Habib said: The jinn in Paradise have with them restrained-gazed women from their own kind of jinn, so the verse negates deflowering by both human and jinn women. Qatadah said: ﴿Ka'annahunna﴾ [as if they were] means in the clearness of rubies and the redness of coral; if you inserted a thread into a ruby and looked at it, you would see it from behind. End of quote. In al-Tirmidhi: "The woman among the women of Paradise, the whiteness of her shin will be seen from behind seventy garments, and its marrow." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Rubies and coral are among the things by whose beauty one is delighted, so they were compared with what is fitting for comparison: the ruby in its smoothness and its translucence, and coral in its smoothness and the beauty of its appearance. In this manner of reflection the Arabs named women after them, such as Durrah bint Abi Lahab and Marjanah, mother of Sa'id. End of quote.

Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿illa al-hisan﴾ [anything but the beautiful ones], meaning by the hisan the wide-eyed maidens (al-hur al-'in).

﴿Wa min dunihima﴾ [And beneath them]: that is, beneath those two gardens in rank and value, ﴿two gardens﴾ are for the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin). The first two are for the foremost (al-sabiqun); this was said by Ibn Zayd and most scholars. Al-Hasan said: The first two are for the foremost, and the latter two for the followers. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿Wa min dunihima﴾ in nearness is for the favoured ones, and the two mentioned later are better than the two mentioned first. This is shown by the fact that He described these two as having gushing springs, and those two only as having flowing streams; and these two as dark green, which is a source of delight, and those two as having branches, and every garden has branches. Al-Zamakhshari preferred this view and said: For the near ones there are two gardens, and beneath them, for the companions of the right, are two gardens dark green from intense greenness. Others preferred the first view, citing the mention of flowing in the two springs (that they gush, not merely flow), and His saying about them: ﴿of every fruit﴾ [55:52], and about the latter two: ﴿therein are fruit﴾; and [the mention of] reclining on what has brocade for its linings, which is the furnishings, while for the latter two the reclining is on the rafraf, which is the edge of the tent; and furnishings prepared for reclining are better. The 'abqari is embroidery and brocade, which is higher than it. What is compared to rubies and coral is better in description than "good and beautiful." The apparent meaning of gushing is with water. Ibn Jubayr said: With musk, ambergris and camphor in the houses of the people of Paradise, as the rain sprinkles. It is also reported from him: with various kinds of fruit and water.

﴿Wa nakhlun wa rummanun﴾ [palm trees and pomegranates]: he connected them with "fruit," and the conjunction implies that they are not included within fruit; this was said by some. Yunus ibn Habib and others said: He repeated them, though they are among the best fruits, to honour them and to point to them, as He said: ﴿and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [2:98]. It was also said: Because the date palm's fruit is both fruit and food, and the pomegranate is fruit and medicine, so they were not reserved purely for fruit-eating.

﴿Fihinna khayratun﴾: the plural of khayrah, an adjective formed on the pattern fa'lah from khayr (good), just as they formed from sharr (evil) the word sharrah. It was also said it is a lightened form of khayyirah, and Bakr ibn Habib, Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi and Ibn Miqsam read it so, meaning with a shadda on the ya'. It is reported from Abu 'Amr with a fatha on the ya', as if it were the plural of khayirah, pluralized on the pattern fa'lah. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) explained this to Umm Salamah, saying: "Those who are good in character, beautiful in faces."

"She is lax toward her neighbours, so they visit her; and she is heedless of her own dwellings, so she is excused."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is within reach.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Therein are those restraining their gaze, whom no man or jinn has touched before them.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿As if they were rubies and coral.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿And beneath them are two other gardens.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Dark green.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Therein are two gushing springs.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Therein are fruit, palm trees and pomegranates.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Therein are good and beautiful [women].﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Maidens restrained in pavilions.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Whom no man or jinn has touched before them.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Reclining on green cushions and beautiful rich carpets.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas said: [They pick it] standing, sitting and lying down; neither distance nor thorns prevent their hand from reaching it.

'Isa [ibn 'Umar] recited ﴿wajna﴾ with a fatha on the jim and a kasra on the nun, as if he inclined the nun (imalah, pronouncing a vowel toward a following sound), even though the alif had been dropped in pronunciation, just as Abu 'Amr inclined in ﴿hatta nara Allah﴾. It was also read as ﴿wajni﴾ with a kasra on the jim. [Note: the Arabic names two qira'ah (recitation variants) here.]

The pronoun in ﴿fihinna﴾ refers to the gardens (al-jinan), which is indicated by "two gardens," since each individual is given two gardens, so it is correct to say that they are many gardens. Even if "the two gardens" is meant literally as the dual, and each category of jinn and humans has one garden, the pronoun refers to what the garden contains of assembly places, palaces and dwellings. It was also said that it refers to the couches (furush), meaning that therein they are prepared for enjoyment; this is a good view and close in its derivation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Therein" refers to these enumerated favours, namely the two gardens, the two springs, the fruit and the harvest. End of quote; but this is far-fetched. Al-Farra' said: Every place in the garden is a garden, which is why it says ﴿fihinna﴾. The word ﴿al-tarf﴾ (gaze) is originally a verbal noun, which is why it is singular. The apparent meaning is that they are the ones who restrict their eyes to their husbands, so they do not look at others. Ibn Zayd said: She says to her husband, "By the might of my Lord, I see nothing in Paradise more beautiful than you." It was also said that ﴿al-tarf﴾ is the gaze of others, meaning that they restrain the eyes of whoever looks at them from looking at anyone else.

﴿Lam yatmithhunna﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: No one has deflowered them before their husbands. It was also said: No one has had intercourse with them in any manner, whether by deflowering or otherwise; this is the view of 'Ikrimah. The pronoun in ﴿qablahum﴾ refers to whoever the pronoun in ﴿muttaki'in﴾ refers to. The majority read ﴿yatmithhunna﴾ with a kasra on the mim in both places. Talhah, 'Isa, the companions of 'Abd Allah and 'Ali read it with a damma. Some read with a damma on the first and a kasra on the second, some with the reverse, some with the option of either, and al-Jahdari read it with a fatha on the mim in both places. The negation of their being touched by humans is clear. As for jinn, Mujahid and al-Hasan said: The wives of humans may be had intercourse with by their husbands when the husband does not mention God Most High, so here the verse negates all who have intercourse. Damrah ibn Habib said: The jinn in Paradise have with them restrained-gazed women from their own kind of jinn, so the verse negates deflowering by both human and jinn women. Qatadah said: ﴿Ka'annahunna﴾ [as if they were] means in the clearness of rubies and the redness of coral; if you inserted a thread into a ruby and looked at it, you would see it from behind. End of quote. In al-Tirmidhi: "The woman among the women of Paradise, the whiteness of her shin will be seen from behind seventy garments, and its marrow." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Rubies and coral are among the things by whose beauty one is delighted, so they were compared with what is fitting for comparison: the ruby in its smoothness and its translucence, and coral in its smoothness and the beauty of its appearance. In this manner of reflection the Arabs named women after them, such as Durrah bint Abi Lahab and Marjanah, mother of Sa'id. End of quote.

Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿illa al-hisan﴾ [anything but the beautiful ones], meaning by the hisan the wide-eyed maidens (al-hur al-'in).
